Consumer complaint narrative:
Summary : After a fraud claim on a store card ( XXXX XXXX, Synchrony had made multiple adjustments on my account, resulting in an overcharge of {$5100.00} more than I owe, plus interest. I have spent hours on multiple calls and Synchronys own representatives have admitted they have overcharged me but failed to correct it. I am requesting that Synchrony immediately remove the {$5100.00} overcharge and any associated interest or fees, given that I was told by Synchronys support rep that I could skip the XXXX payment with no fees or interest while they resolved this issue, but I still accrued {$170.00} in interest. 



Details : On XX/XX/year>, I purchased two items at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, VA ) . The items were one sectional sofa ( 4 pieces ) and one recliner. I financed this purchase with Synchrony Bank using their XXXX XXXX XXXX  offered in store. The financing terms were 12 months deferred interest with payment. This was a brand new card, opened the date of purchase. According to my receipt from XXXX , the total of the two items after taxes were the following : sofa ( {$5100.00} ) and recliner ( {$630.00} ). This summed to {$5800.00} and was the correct amount to be financed.

Several days later, I viewed my account and noticed a discrepancy. I had two separate charges listed on the card. One charge was {$5800.00} ( sofa + recliner ) and the other was {$630.00}. In addition to appearing to be a double charge, the lone {$630.00} charge had other odd discrepancies, such as a different transaction date ( XX/XX/XXXX ) and different location of purchase ( XXXX, Michigan ) than the original. The account balance was {$6400.00}. This was {$630.00} more than my receipt from XXXX XXXX I called Synchrony about this discrepancy and after consulting with a support rep, I filed a fraud claim against the additional {$630.00} charge from XXXX, Michigan. 


While the {$630.00} fraud claim was being investigated, Synchrony opened another account for me. They did not immediately transfer the balance of the original account to this new account. I am not ( to my knowledge ) currently able to access this original account. 


On XX/XX/year>, an adjustment of - {$630.00} and a balance transfer of {$630.00} was made on the new account. This put the account balance at {$0.00}. 


On XX/XX/year>, a XXXX  charge of {$5100.00} was added to the new account. This made me nervous that they thought my fraud claim was against the recliner in general, rather than the claim being against the errant additional {$630.00} charge. On XX/XX/year>, I called Synchrony about this and they indicated that this was a part of the fraud claim process and I needed to wait for the fraud claim to be resolved before Im expected to start making payments. 


On XX/XX/year>, I was sent a letter from Synchrony Bank via email. This letter said that the fraud claim was denied on the following grounds : You authorized, participated in, or benefited from the purchase. They said they reversed the transaction credit ( s ) along with associated interest and fee credits that were provided during the investigation. It appeared that while Synchrony was not acknowledging a change in their charges, they actually may have ended up correcting the charges listed on my account. I was satisfied with that outcome, despite the documentation implying no action was taken on my account. The total amount charged on my account at this point was still only {$5100.00}. 


On XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX, balance adjustments of {$5100.00} and {$630.00} were added to my account, respectively. Because I already had {$5100.00} charged to me on XX/XX/XXXX, this balance adjustment effectively charged me {$5100.00} twice. At this point, the total amount charged on my account was now {$10000.00}, which shouldnt even be possible, given my credit limit on the card was {$8000.00}. 


On XX/XX/year> I called Synchrony to address this issue. After speaking with a support representative, they assured me that they would resolve this errant balance adjustment. Trusting that was true, I went ahead and started making payments on the card just a few days later. 


On XX/XX/year>, I called about the adjustment again. I was assured it was being resolved. 


On XX/XX/year>, two balance adjustments were made in an effort to correct the charges. One balance adjustment removed- {$5100.00} and another removed - {$630.00}. This was an overcorrection by Synchrony. The - {$630.00} adjustment should not have been removed from the account. I did not register this overcorrection at the time, I just saw the balance go down and I was happy. At this point, the total amount charged to my account was {$5100.00}. This was {$630.00} less than my original XXXX charges. 


On XX/XX/year>, I paid the total balance remaining on the card. The account balance was {$0.00} on XX/XX/year>. I was excited to be done with this account, although I did not realize I still technically owed {$630.00} because it was not on my account. I accrued no interest at all at this point and stopped checking on my account status. 


On XX/XX/year>, I received a phone call from Synchrony which went to voicemail. The voicemail indicated that Synchrony was calling about the initial fraud claim, which I knew had already been closed based on the letter I received on XX/XX/XXXX. Also knowing that the account was fully paid down to {$0.00}, I was not worried about calling Synchrony back, in fear that if I did, more confusion could be caused on their side. 


On XX/XX/year> ( the next day ), Synchrony sent me a letter via email claiming they had closed their fraud investigation a second time. Synchrony also made two balance adjustments to my account. One that added {$5100.00} and another that added {$630.00}. By doing this, Synchrony over-adjusted my account by {$5100.00}. I did not realize that this adjustment had been made, as I thought the account was paid off and I had stopped logging into Synchrony or checking emails. At this point, the total amount charged to my account was {$10000.00}. This was {$5100.00} more than my original XXXX charges. 


On XX/XX/year>, Synchrony sent me an automated email stating that I had a payment due on XX/XX/XXXX. The email said my total account balance was {$5800.00}. This was when I realized that my account was no longer {$0.00}. 


On XX/XX/year>, I called Synchrony again. They initially denied the overcharge. I was on the phone with Synchrony for an hour and sixteen minutes. By the end of the phone call, the support representative acknowledged that Synchrony made an error. She confirmed this error with her manager. I was assured that in one or two billing cycles the {$5100.00} would be removed. I was also assured that I could skip that months payment with no interest or late fees while they resolved the issue. She told me she took very detailed notes on my account that detailed these assurances, in case I had to call in again. I warned that if I have to call again, I will file a CFPB claim and/or involve a lawyer. 


On XX/XX/year>, {$170.00} of interest was charged to my account, despite being told that this would not happen. I was hopeful that any future account adjustments would resolve this and waited. 


On XX/XX/year>, Synchrony sent me a letter via email. The letter seems to indicate that the purchase adjustment was denied, but admittedly, Im confused by the wording of the letter. 


On XX/XX/year>, I called Synchrony to check about a status update of the adjustment, given the next payment was due XX/XX/XXXX and I still had not seen a balance adjustment. I told multiple support reps to check the notes that I was told were on the account from my XX/XX/XXXX phone call. None of them looked at the notes so I explained the situation to each of them. After a one hour and thirty minute phone call, the rep acknowledged that Synchrony had over-charged me and that within 7-10 business days ( XX/XX/XXXX ), I should expect the balance to only include the {$630.00} charge plus any interest that accrued. 


On this call, I also told the support rep about the assurance that interest and late fees would not be charged last time I called in XXXX. I told her to check the account notes to confirm. She told me that there were no notes at all from my XX/XX/XXXX phone call and she told me that the guidance I was given about skipping the payment was false. She told me I would still be charged interest for the {$630.00} that I still owed and any account adjustments would not affect that amount. This is a violation of Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices ( UDAAP ).

I have no confidence that Synchrony will correct their errors after 5 months of back and forth with the company. I need help fighting this corrupt company.

This complaint concerns false and contradictory statements made by JPMorgan Chase Bank in their response to my previous CFPB case number XXXX. I am filing this as a new complaint because Chase materially misrepresented facts to the CFPB and continues to unlawfully withhold my closing funds. 

Chase closed my business checking account ( ending XXXX ) on XX/XX/year>, with a balance of approximately {$22000.00}. The official Chase account statement shows a XXXX XXXX Check Charge, confirming that a closing check was issued and the account brought to XXXX. This means the funds were processed as payable to me, not subject to any ongoing investigation. 

After I provided a detailed written explanation of all deposits at Chases request, I received a voicemail from the Chase Executive Office on XX/XX/year>. In that message, a representative named XXXX XXXX stated : I am calling from the Executive Office regarding the letter that you sent us. I do want to advise that regarding this matter, the bank will not be releasing any funds again. We are sorry for the outcome, and this is our final decision. We are exercising our rights under the terms of our deposit agreement. This message explicitly referenced my letter of explanation and confirmed Chase had completed its review and made a final decision. No request for additional information or documentation followed. 

However, in Chases written response to the CFPB, the bank stated : We closed your account on XX/XX/year>, and placed {$22000.00} in suspense. We are still conducting our research and do not have a time frame on when this will be resolved. These statements contradict both Chases own voicemail and its XX/XX/year>XXXX  account statement. A bank can not both close an account and continue to investigate or suspend funds afterward. Once closed, Chase no longer has contractual authority under Section IX ( C ) of its Deposit Account Agreement to hold funds. That clause only applies to active accounts under restriction, not closed ones. 

Chases contradictory responses and shifting explanations indicate bad faith and potential misrepresentation in a federal regulatory proceeding. The suspense claim appears to be an internal accounting device, not a lawful reason to retain funds indefinitely. The voicemail and account statement prove that the banks investigation had already concluded months before it told the CFPB otherwise. 

I am requesting that the CFPB open a new review into this matter and require Chase to ( 1 ) explain the legal authority it claims to hold funds after account closure, ( 2 ) provide documentation of any ongoing investigation or internal suspense record, and ( 3 ) immediately release my {$22000.00} closing balance or provide lawful written justification for refusal. These inconsistencies and misrepresentations warrant independent review and regulatory scrutiny.

Subject : Barclays ' failure to investigate reported fraud, issue provisional credit, and comply with consumer protection laws. 

To Whom It May Concern, I am filing this complaint against Barclays Bank for their failure to protect consumers, investigate fraud reports, and comply with federal regulations under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act ( EFTA ) and Regulation Z. 

On XX/XX/year>, I reported fraudulent charges on my Barclays credit card through their automated fraud reporting system. The automated message stated that my claim was received and that no further action was required on my part. However, since that date : Barclays has not contacted me or provided any written confirmation, case number, or update regarding my fraud report. 

I never received a provisional credit, as required by law when fraud is reported in good faith. 

The online fraud reporting portal produces repeated error messages, preventing follow-up submissions. 

When I contacted Barclays directly to expedite the issue, I was told it could not be escalated to a senior analyst, and that I would receive a callback within XXXX hours which never occurred. 

Barclays has continued to charge interest and fees on fraudulent transactions, which is illegal and unethical. 

These repeated failures show a complete lack of compliance with consumer protection standards. Their automated systems provide false reassurance to customers that a fraud report is complete, while in reality, no investigation or credit adjustment occurs. This pattern of neglect directly violates the consumers right to dispute unauthorized transactions and to be protected from financial harm during the investigation period. 

I am requesting that the CFPB : Investigate Barclays fraud and dispute resolution practices for systemic noncompliance. 

Require Barclays to remove all fraudulent charges and reverse all interest or late fees tied to them.

Each time I called, I received a different explanation one representative said the account was restricted, another said closed, and another said paid-off. 

On XX/XX/year>, I spoke with another representative who acknowledged that the account had an overdraft that had been due for years. I told him that I understood there had been an overdraft, but I reminded him that several Capital One employees told me the debt was past seven years and legally uncollectible. Capital Ones handling of this account from the original promise that I could keep it open by making payments, to later telling me it was uncollectible and refunding only part of what was owed shows a clear pattern of miscommunication and inconsistent internal procedures. These actions constitute an unauthorized collection on a time-barred account and a potential Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) and Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ( FDCPA ) violation. 

I am submitting this full and final statement so that the CFPB investigators and Capital Ones compliance department have a complete and accurate timeline of events, including the evidence I have ( my screenshot showing the restricted-to-closed status change and detailed notes from my conversations ).

FTC Used Car Rule ( 16 CFR 455 ) requires dealers to disclose known defects and damage history on the Buyers Guide ; 3. This has resulted in significant damage to my credit profile, unnecessary exposure to identity theft risks, and a blatant disregard for fair lending practices and customer security. I demand a thorough investigation into Barclays ' practices, immediate rectification of my account, and appropriate penalties against the bank for their reckless behavior. 
I have been a Barclays customer for over XXXX years, holding their JetBlue credit card during this entire period. Throughout this time, I have made every payment on time and in full, maintaining an exemplary account history. My credit score exceeds XXXX, and I hold multiple other credit cards with aggregate limits surpassing {$100000.00}, demonstrating my strong financial standing and creditworthiness. 

The issues began when I attempted to book a JetBlue flight and was presented with a promotion for the JetBlue PLUS card, which offered enhanced benefits. Given my longstanding relationship with Barclays and my existing JetBlue card, I reasonably assumed an upgrade would be straightforward without impacting my credit report. I contacted Barclays customer service by phone to inquire about upgrading my account. To my surprise, the representative informed me that no upgrade option was available and that I must apply for an entirely new card online. I expressed concern about the hard credit inquiry this would trigger, which could negatively affect my credit score, but was assured this was the only path forward. Reluctantly, I proceeded with the online application. 

The application resulted in instant approval, but it was flagged for additional verification. A Barclays representative called me to gather more information. I provided and verified all requested details, including my date of birth, Social Security number, existing card number, address, and annual income of {$600000.00}, which they initially questioned as a potential error, despite it being accurate and verifiable. After this verification, the representative proposed closing my existing JetBlue card with its {$25000.00} credit limit, transferring that limit to the new JetBlue PLUS card, and issuing the new card immediately. I voiced strong objections, as this would result in XXXX major negative impacts on my credit : the closure of a long-standing account ( reducing my average account age and available credit ) and a new hard inquiry. However, the representative insisted this was the sole option, leading me to agree under duress. 

The representative then proceeded to close my existing account before finalizing the new one. This was a catastrophic error in process that left me vulnerable. Before completing the transfer, I was transferred to a security department representative, whom I can only describe as unprofessional and obstructive. Despite providing the exact same verification information, and more, this individual claimed they could not confirm my identity. They demanded that I mail physical copies of highly sensitive documents through the U.S. Postal Service : my Social Security card ( front and back ), driver 's license, passport, and a utility bill as proof of address. I immediately raised alarms about the severe identity theft risks this posed, especially given the insecure nature of postal mail and my prior experience with identity theft. Barclays ' insistence on this archaic and dangerous method is not only outdated but recklessly endangers customers in an era of rampant data breaches and fraud. 

I made over XXXX subsequent calls to Barclays, arguing with multiple representatives about the absurdity of this policy. Each time, I was told there was " absolutely no way '' to submit documents securely via electronic means, such as encrypted email or a secure upload portal. These are standard practices at virtually every other financial institution. Finally, after persistent escalation, one supervisor begrudgingly authorized submission via fax. Ironically, this was a method similar to one that led to my identity being stolen in the past. I faxed copies of my passport, driver 's license, and utility bills as requested. 

Unbelievably, Barclays then deemed this insufficient and doubled down, demanding a mailed photocopy of my Social Security card 's front and back. This final demand was the breaking point. I refused to comply, as it would compound the already unacceptable risks to my personal security. As a direct result of Barclays ' incompetence and inflexible policies, my credit has suffered XXXX major derogatory marks : ( XXXX ) the closure of my longstanding {$25000.00} credit line, reducing my total available credit and harming my utilization ratio ; ( XXXX ) the loss of that credit line 's positive history from my credit report ; and ( XXXX ) the hard inquiry from the new application, which remains unresolved because Barclays has not approved the card due to my refusal to mail sensitive documents. Had Barclays disclosed the full ramifications upfront or offered a simple upgrade without closure, I would never have proceeded. Their misleading representations and procedural failures have directly caused this damage. 

Barclays ' actions exhibit egregious behavior, including prematurely closing accounts without proper safeguards, misleading customers about application processes, and enforcing outdated verification methods that prioritize internal bureaucracy over customer safety. These practices pose significant risks to customers, such as heightened vulnerability to identity theft through insecure document transmission, unwarranted damage to credit scores that can lead to higher interest rates on future loans or denials of credit, and unnecessary financial stress from lost credit availability. Numerous complaints filed with the CFPB and BBB highlight similar issues with Barclays ' handling of fraud and verification, underscoring a pattern of negligence that endangers consumers ' financial well-being.

This tactic exemplifies their egregious behavior by withholding transparency and documentation that consumers are entitled to under federal regulations, further exposing me to prolonged credit uncertainty and potential fraud risks. Such refusal violates the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) requirements for timely and written adverse action notices, as well as the Consumer Financial Protection Act 's prohibitions against unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts that hinder consumers ' ability to resolve disputes efficiently. 

Furthermore, these actions violate several key consumer protection laws. By closing my account prematurely and reporting it to credit bureaus without ensuring the new card could be issued, Barclays may have breached the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), which requires accuracy in credit reporting and proper notice for adverse actions affecting credit. Their refusal to provide secure, electronic document submission options contravenes the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act ( GLBA ), specifically its Safeguards Rule, which mandates that financial institutions implement reasonable measures to protect sensitive customer information from unauthorized access or misuse. Insisting on mailing highly sensitive documents like Social Security cards exposes customers to fraud risks, potentially constituting an unfair or deceptive act under the Consumer Financial Protection Act and FTC regulations. This not only fails to safeguard nonpublic personal information but also smacks of predatory tactics that exploit customers ' trust. Such violations undermine the integrity of the financial system and warrant severe penalties to deter future misconduct.

Issue: Problem caused by your funds being low
Consumer complaint narrative:
On XX/XX/year>, a sheriff XXXX XXXX was served on my bank. At the time, the business account balance was not sufficient to cover the levy. Instead of leaving the legally required protected amount, the bank froze more funds than were available and pushed the account into a negative balance. This violates California Code of Civil Procedure section 704.220, which prohibits a bank from overdrafting an account when executing a levy and requires an automatic exemption amount to remain available for support. 

Because the levy created a negative balance, multiple automatic transactions that normally would have been declined were instead processed against the negative balance. As a result, the bank charged repeated overdraft fees across several business accounts beginning on XX/XX/XXXX and continuing through XXXX. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, I contacted the banks XXXX Department. The representative confirmed the issue, acknowledged the XXXX XXXX concern, and entered a notation in my account. No one followed up after that call. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, the banks system re-posted or re-dated the levy, which created additional negative impact and caused more overdraft fees. This was not a new levy, but an internal system action by the bank. 

I sent secure messages through online banking requesting an explanation, a review of the levy processing error, and reversal of all overdraft fees caused by the negative balance created by the levy. I also requested escalation to the banks Executive Resolution department. The bank has not corrected the issue.

I have already filed a formal Claim of Exemption with the sheriffs department responsible for the levy, and that claim is pending. In the meantime, the bank is continuing to charge overdraft fees that were directly caused by XXXX processing errors, not by customer transactions or misuse. 

California Code of Civil Procedure section 704.220 requires banks to automatically leave a protected minimum amount in a deposit account when processing a levy. This exemption applies to all individuals and sole proprietors and does not require any filing by the account holder. The bank may not take funds below the protected minimum and may not overdraft an account while executing a levy. At the time the levy was applied, the balance in the account was not sufficient to cover the levy, yet the bank froze the entire balance and pushed the account into a negative amount. This violated the automatic exemption under CCP 704.220 and directly caused the subsequent overdraft fees and negative balances across multiple business accounts. 

This situation has caused severe financial hardship, and the bank has not provided a meaningful explanation or resolution despite multiple attempts to address the issue.

Sub-issue: Funds not received from closed account
Consumer complaint narrative:
Dear Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, I am filing an official complaint against Bank of America , N.A . for unlawfully freezing and withholding my business funds, closing my account without proper notice, and refusing to return {$47000.00} in legitimate deposited check funds that are not connected to any merchant activity. 

1. Summary of the Issue I held a Bank of America business checking account linked to a merchant services account. My verified balance at the moment of closure was {$87000.00} : {$40000.00} came from merchant transactions. 

{$47000.00} came from a separate check deposit, unrelated to merchant processing. 

Bank of America froze the entire {$87000.00}, including funds that have no connection to merchant transactions or chargebacks. After freezing the funds, the bank closed my account and stated they would mail me a check for the balance. I have not received any funds, and the bank is unlawfully holding both the merchant deposits and my separate check deposit. 

2. Why Bank of Americas Actions Are Unlawful A. Improper Freezing of Non-Merchant Funds Even if the bank claims to investigate merchant activity, they can not legally freeze deposited check funds that are not related to merchant transactions. 

Under : 12 CFR 1005 ( Regulation E ) Financial institutions must give written notice, specific reasons, and legally valid justification when restricting access to funds. 

The bank did not provide any written explanation for freezing the {$47000.00} in check deposit funds. 

B. Violation of UCC Article 4 Duties Regarding Deposited Checks Under the Uniform Commercial Code, Article 4, once a deposited check has cleared, the bank must : Make funds available OR return them to the account holder upon account closure A bank may not permanently confiscate or hold cleared deposits without a government seizure order, court order, or lawful restriction notice. 

Bank of America provided none of these. 

C. Violation of FDIC Rules on Account Closures and Fund Disbursement Per FDIC guidance, when a bank closes an account : It must notify the customer It must return the remaining balance promptly Funds can not be held indefinitely without legal justification Bank of America closed my account and has failed to disburse any portion of the {$87000.00}.

D. Violation of Consumer Financial Protection Act ( 12 U.S.C. 5531 ) UDAAP Bank of Americas conduct constitutes : Unfair practices : Freezing all funds without cause Deceptive practices : Claiming they would send my check but never doing so Abusive practices : Blocking access to the {$47000.00} check deposit that has nothing to do with merchant processing This is a direct violation of federal standards prohibiting Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices.

E. Failure to Provide Required Adverse Action Notice When a bank closes a business account due to alleged risk, they must provide a written adverse action or risk notice. 

Bank of America did not provide : Any written explanation Any investigation record Any legal basis for holding the {$47000.00} check deposit 3. Harm To My Business Bank of Americas actions have caused significant financial harm : The entire {$87000.00} remains frozen without explanation The {$47000.00} deposited check, which is not merchant-related, is being illegally withheld The bank closed my account without properly disbursing my funds My business operations have been severely disrupted

Those statements conflict with the credit bureau reporting. 

The checking account tied to autopay was a customer-initiated closure request. I was told to wait until the fraud dispute was resolved before closing it. However, after the dispute was resolved in my favor, American Express moved forward with closing the account and cutting a check without honoring my request to pause the closure so I could transfer the funds electronically. 

Call XXXX on XX/XX/year> ( all times approximate ) : XXXXXXXX XXXX ( XXXX min, XXXX ) : The Amex Checking team confirmed the fraud dispute was resolved in my favor, confirmed the checking closure was customer-initiated, and confirmed a check was sent for the credited funds. 

XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX ) : A senior supervisor on the XXXX team, identifying as Them with ID XXXX, stated she had authority to close the Platinum Card. This notification failure is particularly egregious because Bank of America has records of my prior support calls regarding difficulties with their malfunctioning bill pay system. Their Autopay system did not work and the scheduled bill pay was the only way to pay your credit card. They were aware their broken system made it difficult to set up. Despite this knowledge, they removed my scheduled bill pay without adequate safeguards or verification that I was aware. After it was removed without my knowledge there was a single missed payment, which was obviously not due to financial inability or unwillingness to pay, it was the direct and foreseeable result of Bank of America 's inadequate system change.

The moment I discovered the missed payment, I immediately paid the full past-due amount. I escalated this matter to Bank of America 's escalation management and explained the situation. I requested they either remove the inaccurate late payment from my credit report or submit an emergency off-cycle credit bureau update reflecting the account as current given the time-sensitive mortgage closing. They categorically refused both requests, despite the late payment being directly caused by their system migration, their failure to provide clear notice after the scheduled bill pay was canceled, and their failure to notify me that the payment was overdue. This occurred despite my perfect payment history prior to the system change, my immediate payment upon discovering the issue, the fact that this was a system-wide problem affecting multiple customers, and the severe and imminent harm to my mortgage closing. 

Bank of America is furnishing information to credit bureaus that misrepresents my creditworthiness. The late payment on my credit report suggests I am unable or unwilling to pay my debts, when in reality I maintained perfect payment history and only missed a payment because Bank of America removed my scheduled bill pay and did not notify properly. This is not an accurate reflection of my credit risk or payment behavior. Bank of America created this problem through their own system migration and notification failures, yet they are punishing me by refusing to correct the inaccurate credit reporting. They had a duty to either maintain scheduled billpay functionality during migration or provide clear, multi-channel notice that autopay was canceled. They did neither. I could not reasonably avoid this injury because I was not adequately informed autopay was removed. The late payment does not reflect my true creditworthiness or payment intent, and Bank of America 's own actions directly caused the late payment as a foreseeable consequence of their inadequate notification practices.

1. The resolution letter dated XX/XX/year> stated : we found that no fraud occurred, or that the transactions were authorized. However, the supporting documentation only confirmed authorization, not the absence of fraud. Under the FTC Act ( 15 U.S.C. 45 ), fraud includes misrepresentation and unfair practices, not just lack of authorization. Mastercard Rules ( Section 5.9.2 ) also prohibit merchants from submitting transactions that are illegal under applicable law. Therefore, the documentation does not establish that fraud was absent. 

XXXX. The XXXX applied was XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX  In reality, the merchant provided gambling services. Gambling transactions must be coded under XXXX XXXX ( XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX  ). Misclassification constitutes transactional misrepresentation under Mastercard Rules ( Section 5.8.1 Merchants must accurately describe the goods or services provided and must not misrepresent the nature of the transaction ). Incorrect XXXX coding is grounds for chargeback under XXXX XXXX XXXX, Reason Code XXXX ( Cardholder Dispute Misrepresentation ). 

XXXX. The supporting documentation acknowledged that the merchantis banned in New Jersey. Despite this, the denial concluded that authorization alone negates fraud. Under New Jersey law ( N.J.S.A. 2C:371 et seq. ), sweepstakes gambling is prohibited. Mastercard Rules ( Section 5.9.2 ) explicitly prohibit merchants from processing transactions that are illegal in the cardholders jurisdiction. Supporting an illegal merchant conflicts with both state law and Mastercard compliance obligations. 

4. Please confirm whether an investigation into merchant misrepresentation and illegal activity was conducted. Mastercard Rules ( Section 3.11 ) require issuers to investigate merchant misrepresentation and illegal activity when disputes are raised. The documentation provided does not demonstrate such review.

5. Finally, please clarify whether Wells Fargos position is that any customer authorization renders a transaction valid, even when merchant identity and activity are misrepresented. Under CFPB Regulation E ( 12 C.F.R. 1005.2 ( m ) ), authorization must be informed and valid. A yes response obtained through misrepresentation does not constitute lawful authorization. The FTC Act ( 15 U.S.C. 45 ) prohibits deceptive practices, and Mastercard Chargeback Guide ( Reason Code 4837 No Cardholder Authorization ) recognizes that misrepresentation invalidates consumer consent.

Thank you for your attention to this matter. I respectfully request a full reconsideration of the dispute in light of these points.

Consumer complaint narrative:
Subject : Synchrony Bank Failure to Conduct a Reasonable Investigation, Fraud Alert System Failures, and Communication Errors. 
I am filing a new complaint regarding Synchrony Banks continued mishandling of a clear case of credit card fraud involving unauthorized transactions on my compromised Groupon account. My prior CFPB complaint, XXXX, was closed based on Synchronys incomplete and inadequate response, but the underlying fraud remains unresolved. 
Synchrony Bank has repeatedly denied my dispute despite clear evidence of account compromise, multiple investigative failures, a malfunction of their fraud alert system, and significant communication errors within their fraud department. 
My XXXX account was accessed by an unauthorized party on XX/XX/XXXX, and multiple purchases were made without my knowledge or consent using my Synchrony credit card. I reported the fraud to Synchrony immediately the same day. The account was closed, and an investigation was initiated. Since then, Synchrony has issued multiple denials based on incorrect assumptions, incomplete investigative steps, and inaccurate claims regarding my submission of documentation. 
I also requested that XXXX permanently close my account to stop further fraudulent activity, as I was unable to change my password. It took several days for XXXX to complete my request, leaving the account vulnerable.

1. Improper reliance on email delivery to claim authorization. 
Synchrony claimed the transactions were authorized because confirmation emails were delivered to my inbox. This demonstrates a misunderstanding of how XXXX functions. 
Groupon vouchers are stored and redeemable directly from the XXXX account, regardless of whether emails are accessed. Email delivery does not control access to vouchers and does not prove that I authorized or completed any transaction. I had not accessed my XXXX account since XX/XX/XXXX. The only reason I found out about the fraud was because my XXXX account was not compromised. 
XXXX on email copies as proof of authorization does not meet the Regulation Z requirement for a reasonable investigation. 

2. Failure to verify login/IP/device data standard in digital-goods fraud cases. 
Synchrony closed my dispute without obtaining or reviewing login history, device fingerprints, or IP addresses from XXXX. As I stated multiple times, no one in my household made these transactions, and any IP used could belong to a VPN or system-generated address, not me. 
Synchrony relied instead on a XXXX note referencing a partial AVS match and a location within XXXX mile of the billing city. A partial AVS match does not establish cardholder authorization, and a location within XXXX mile of the billing city could easily reflect a VPN or system IP, not the authorized cardholder. 

3. Fraud-Alert System Failures.

Synchrony Banks fraud-alert system failed completely during the fraudulent activity, despite historically sending me alerts for much smaller or less suspicious transactions. The failure appears to result from multiple systemic flaws : Merchant misclassification XXXX is likely treated as a low-risk merchant, causing the system to under-prioritize alerts for unusual activity. 
Repeated transactions of the same amount done within short period of time to the same vendor ignored failed to trigger alerts, even though this pattern is highly suspicious. 
Timing of transactions XXXX occurred between XXXX AM and XXXX AM, which is unusual to my transaction history, and therefore fraud detection sensitivity must be enhanced, but failed instead. 
Partial AVS match misinterpreted A partial address verification match should have raised a red flag, but the system incorrectly treated it as sufficient authorization. 
Digital-goods vulnerability Digital purchases like XXXX vouchers are incorrectly categorized as low-risk, resulting in weak monitoring for unauthorized activity. 
Algorithmic inconsistency Historically, alerts were sent for legitimate purchases under similar circumstances, showing the system did not function properly on the night of the fraud. 
These failures demonstrate that Synchrony Banks internal fraud detection and alert systems were inadequate, inconsistent, and not functioning as promised, placing the burden of risk entirely on me as the account holder. 

4. Inaccurate statements about documentation & systemic communication failures.

In its most recent denial, Synchrony claimed that I did not provide the requested information, which is false.

I submitted all documents using their prepaid envelope, as directed. Their fax number was nonfunctional, and their PO Box provides no tracking, meaning consumers can not confirm receipt. I alerted Synchrony bank about the issue multiple times. During a phone call, a Synchrony representative admitted that documents were not easily accessible or not properly attached to my case internally. Synchrony ignored these system failures and incorrectly blamed me. 

5. Improper and harmful credit reporting.

Synchrony has reported delinquency for charges that are still under dispute. My credit score dropped from XXXX to XXXX, causing financial harm. Reporting negative information while a fraud dispute remains unresolved is improper.

Goldman Sachs did not address the photographic evidence, the chat logs, or my detailed written statement. 2. Ensure the newly submitted evidence is thoroughly reviewed.

Consumer complaint narrative:
Barclays is reporting an inaccurate Date of First Delinquency ( DOFD ) on my Barclays XXXX XXXX, and their XX/XX/XXXX letter contains multiple factual and legal errors showing improper re-aging. 

My account was permanently closed in XXXX, and I had continuous rolling delinquencies leading up to that closure, including 90120 day lates. After the account was already closed, Barclays placed me into a reduced-payment hardship plan in early XXXX. 

Under the FCRA and XXXX  guidelines, the DOFD is a fixed, immovable date. It is the date of the first missed payment in a continuous delinquency, and it can not be changed by modified terms, hardship plans, payment plans, or charge-off status. A payment plan can update account status, but it can not reset the DOFD in any circumstance unless the account is fully brought current under original terms, which never happened. Barclays admits in writing that I was on modified terms and never brought current.

Barclays claims that entering the hardship plan changed my DOFD to XXXX. This is legally incorrect. Since the payment plan occurred after the account was closed, the DOFD can not restart or move forward. A closed account can not generate a new delinquency period under XXXX  rules.

Barclays is also incorrectly implying that DOFD is flexible until charge-off. This is not true. Once an account is permanently closed, the original DOFD is locked in and can not be moved. DOFD is not determined at charge-off it is determined at the first mispayment in the continuous series of delinquencies that led to closure.

Barclays explanation closely resembles confusing the statute of limitations with DOFD, which are two separate legal concepts. DOFD governs credit reporting ; the statute of limitations governs collections. Payment plans do not reset the DOFD.

The fact that Barclays continues to insist on a DOFD after account closure suggests they are improperly attempting to re-age the account. Re-aging debt or reporting a false DOFD violates FCRA 623 ( a ) ( 5 ).

Requested Resolution : 1. Correct the DOFD to the original delinquency in XXXX  ( or earlier ).

2. Correct the removal date based on the accurate DOFD.

3. Remove any re-aged or inaccurate reporting.

4. Delete the tradeline entirely if Barclays can not verify the true DOFD with documentation.

5. I request CFPB oversight due to repeated incorrect explanations and inconsistent application of XXXX  rules.

I am filing a complaint against Navy Federal Credit Union for : ( 1 ) failure to provide the required verbal disclosures during a dispute call, ( 2 ) improper reversal of a provisional credit without effective advance notice, and ( 3 ) unauthorized right-of-offset withdrawals that caused financial harm. 

I contacted Navy Federal by phone regarding a XXXX dispute. The representative handled the entire dispute process and submitted the claim for me over the phone, which meant I did not have the opportunity to view or acknowledge the disclosures I normally would have seen if I had filed online. This includes the required warning that the credit issued is temporary, may be reversed, and could impact my account. Because the dispute was filed by phone, verbal disclosure was required, but none was provided. 

The provisional credit amount was approximately {$400.00}, and Navy Federal later swept {$0.00} from my savings account using right-of-offset after the reversal pushed my account negative.

A Navy Federal supervisor later reviewed the call recording and confirmed to me directly that the representative never verbally disclosed that the credit was temporary, never explained that it could be reversed, and never warned me that my account balance could be affected. The supervisor acknowledged that I was not verbally informed of any of these required details. 

After the call, I relied on the representatives explanation and acted in good faith. When I checked my app ( as instructed by the representative ) and saw the funds in my account, I reasonably believed the dispute was resolved and sent the money to the correct XXXX recipient based on the verbal communication and the updated balance shown in my app. At this point, I still had not seen any email notices. 

I later received a push notification from the Navy Federal mobile app informing me that my account was overdrawn. This was the first time I became aware that the provisional credit had been reversed. Navy Federal keeps insisting that they emailed me notice, but the harm occurred before any email could have prevented anything. Written notice does not satisfy the requirement for effective notice when the consumer relied on verbal communication and the representative failed to disclose essential information during the call. 

Furthermore, Regulation E ( 1005.11 ( d ) ( 2 ) ) requires that if an institution does not give proper advance notice of a provisional credit reversal, it must protect the consumer from overdraft harm for five business days. Navy Federal did neither. Instead, after my balance went negative from the reversal, Navy Federal also used right-of-offset to withdraw funds from my savings account without any verbal warning or effective notice, which increased the harm.

I respectfully request that CFPB require Navy Federal to : 1. Reverse the overdraft caused by the improper reversal of the provisional credit. 
2. Reverse and return the right-of-offset sweep taken from my savings account.

3. Restore my checking and savings accounts to their proper balances.

4. Correct their dispute-handling procedures so that consumers receive proper verbal disclosure when disputes are filed by phone.

5. Ensure Navy Federal complies with Regulation E and CFPBs effective-notice standards.

I acted responsibly and in good faith based on the information I was given. This harm was caused solely by Navy Federals failure to provide the required verbal disclosures and failure to give effective notice before debiting the provisional credit.

Issue Title : Bank of America account access blocked for a non-U.S. resident ; no reasonable way to regain access Complaint Details : I am the lawful owner of a Bank of America checking and savings account. I currently live outside the United States and do not have a U.S. mobile phone number. My account has been kept active for years through occasional small internal transfers ( around {$10.00} between checking and savings ) to prevent it from becoming dormant. I have never performed any suspicious or unusual transactions, nor have I ever transferred funds out of the account since leaving the U.S. 
Because I can no longer receive U.S. text messages, I contacted Bank of America to ask for an alternative verification method. I clearly stated that I am the lawful account holder but unable to maintain a U.S. mobile number, and I asked how I could continue to access and use my account securely. 

USB Security Key issue Bank of America advised me that a USB Security Key could be used instead of SMS verification. Following this guidance, I purchased a USB Security Key and attempted to register it through my Online Banking profile. During the setup process, I was prompted to call customer service to obtain an authorization code. 
I called and successfully passed the identity verification process. However, the representative informed me that, for unclear reasons, she was unable to generate the authorization code. She also suggested that I might need a debit card for this process. After hearing this, I attempted to request a debit card through Online Banking, but the system displayed a message stating that I was not eligible and that the request could not be completed, without explaining why. I then called again and tried once more to register my USB Security Key, but this time the representative told me that a U.S. phone number is required, which I do not have. 
As a result, I was unable to register the USB Security Key at all, and I still had no working method to receive verification codes. 

Attempt to switch to email verification Because I could not complete the USB Security Key registration, I contacted Bank of Americas support team on XXXX again and explained that I had no way to authenticate myself by phone. I asked for the issue to be escalated. 
On XX/XX/XXXX, a representative called me directly. During the call, he removed my outdated U.S. phone number from the system and set my email address as my primary contact method. He told me that it might take some time to take effect. 
However, even after waiting two to three weeks, nothing changed. Whenever I attempted any normal account actionssuch as registering for Mobile Banking, attempting to set up the USB Security Key again, or performing other basic operationsthe system still required a verification code and continued to offer only the phone option. No option for email verification ever appeared. 

Lockout after linking an external bank Because I still could not perform any normal actions on my Bank of America account due to the verification issue, I attempted to link an external bank account as an alternative way to manage my funds. My intention was to create an ACH connection so that, if necessary, I could transfer my own money from Bank of America to my other bank account and indirectly regain some ability to access or use my funds. 
On XX/XX/XXXX, the external link was successfully established through my other bank, and I initiated a small {$10.00} transfer from the other bank, which pulled the funds from my Bank of America account. Within the next one to two days, my Online Banking access stopped working. Although I can still enter my username and password correctly, the system forces me to a Recover User ID or Password page and then rejects my correct account number and SSN as not matching the records. 
On XX/XX/XXXX, after still being unable to log in, I contacted Bank of Americas support team on XXXX again to report the issue. On XX/XX/XXXX, a representative called me, but she informed me that she did not have access to view the current status of my account and could not determine why my correct account number and SSN were being rejected. She stated that, due to system limitations, she had no additional ways to authenticate me and therefore could not assist further. Once again, I was told that the only possible solution was to visit a Bank of America branch in person in the United States. As of XX/XX/XXXX, my Online Banking access remains completely locked, and the issue has not been resolved. 

Reason for requesting CFPB assistance Bank of America has effectively locked me out of my own account and my own funds, while at the same time : * providing no practical way for a non-U.S. resident to verify identity remotely; * giving contradictory and unworkable instructions ( USB Security Key recommended, then blocked ; email set as primary, but no email option appears ) ; and * insisting on an in-person U.S. branch visit, which is impossible for me as a non-U.S. resident. 
I am willing to provide my passport, copies of my previous passport, or any reasonable identification the bank may require. However, no department so far has been able to offer a method for me to submit such documentation or restore access.

Unfortunately, the banker did not mention that the check required an endorsement from the mortgage company listed on it. Additionally, my assistant did not notice that the mortgage company had not signed the check. The banker proceeded with the deposit, and at that time, my online banking reflected that the funds would be available within the next 57 days. 

The following week, when I checked my account, I discovered that it had been restricted. I immediately contacted Chase to determine the cause. I was informed that the bank needed to verify all parties named on the check before releasing the funds. Chase confirmed the endorsements from both homeowners ; however, they stated that they also needed to verify the mortgage company through a direct phone number. I explained that the mortgage company is a large corporation with department-based communication, and it would be unlikely for me to obtain a direct contact person. 

Chase insisted that they would not release the funds until the mortgage company confirmed the check. I then contacted the mortgage company to request the required verification, and they informed me that they do not confirm checks over the phone. They stated that the only way they could endorse or confirm a check would be if the bank sent them a legal copy of the check for endorsement.

I relayed this information to Chase, but the bank stated that they could not send a legal copy because it was against their internal policies. I then requested that Chase return the funds to the insurance company so that a new check could be issued and properly endorsed. Chase informed me that they could not return the funds unless the insurance company directly requested the refund.

I subsequently contacted the insurance company, but they advised me that because the funds were already in the banks possession, they were unable to request them back. I called Chase again and communicated what the insurance company stated. Chase then informed me that they would keep the funds and suggested that I ask the mortgage company for an exception to their policies. I explained that the mortgage company does not make exceptions, just as Chase does not, and requested any alternative solution. Navy Federal Credit Union denied my debit card dispute and improperly classified it in order to avoid following federal Regulation E requirements. They are refusing to process my dispute as an unauthorized electronic fund transfer, even though the merchant delivered the merchandise to the wrong address an address that is not mine which means I received no benefit from the transaction. 

I filed a dispute for a {$52.00} debit card transaction with XXXX XXXX ( purchase date XX/XX/year> ). The merchant delivered the package to an incorrect address that does not match the address on my order. XXXX XXXX and I both provided Navy Federal with pictures and proof showing the actual address where it was delivered. 

Instead of processing the claim under Regulation E, Navy Federal classified my dispute as a non-receipt of merchandise issue under Section 17 of their debit card disclosure, which they say is not governed by Regulation E. They acknowledged this in their written message to me on XX/XX/year>. 

This classification is incorrect. Under 12 CFR 1005.2 ( m ), a transaction is considered unauthorized if it was initiated without my authority and I received no benefit. Because the merchant delivered to an address I do not control, I received XXXX benefit. This makes the transaction an unauthorized electronic fund transfer, which is governed by Regulation E.

Law Violated : Electronic Fund Transfer Act ( EFTA ) Regulation E ( 12 CFR 1005.11 ) Unauthorized transfer definition : 12 CFR 1005.2 ( m ) Navy Federal is refusing to treat this as an unauthorized transaction even though I did not receive the goods and did not benefit from the transfer.

Consumer complaint narrative:
On XX/XX/XXXX, I transferred {$30000.00} into a SoFi high yield savings account after seeing SoFis promotional language stating Supercharge your savings and earn up to 4.30 % APY and Earn up to 4.30 % APY on the account opening page. These statements appeared prominently and implied that opening the account would provide access to the advertised APY. The conditions were not clearly presented on the pages I accessed when I signed up for the account. 

After depositing the funds, I discovered that my APY was conditional on meeting recurring XXXXday requirements that were not made clear upfront. The requirement shown to me only after depositing stated : To keep earning our highest APY *, at least XXXX account holder must complete XXXX of the following : Receive a direct deposit every XXXXDay Evaluation Period, Deposit {$5000.00} or more every XXXXDay Evaluation Period, Pay the SoFi XX/XX/XXXX subscription fee every XX/XX/XXXX days. This requirement was never presented clearly before my deposit. 

I contacted SoFi support. My initial message said : Hi. I need help immediately. The APY requirements on my account were not clearly disclosed when I opened it. I am filing a CFPB complaint about misleading presentation of the rate terms, and Im preparing to move all my funds out as soon as they clear unless this can somehow be resolved. 

When the agent asked what requirements I was referring to, I pasted their own APY condition text. I told them : I would never knowingly agree to a savings rate that requires paying a subscription fee. That is XXXX of the least consumer-friendly practices Ive ever seen. The requirement was buried and absolutely not presented in a clear or prominent way. 

The SoFi representative responded : Yes that is really the requirements of sofi to get the highest apy. 

Later, the supervisor said : These are the requirements for maintaining our highest available APY and they are not able to be changed. 

During the escalation process, I stated : It was not presented clearly on the pages I accessed to sign up for the account and requested a resolution. I asked them clearly for confirmation : I want confirmation that you will maintain my current APY for this evaluation period without requiring a SoFi XX/XX/XXXX subscription or any additional qualifying deposit. 

They refused and reiterated that the APY conditions could not be changed. 

At no point did SoFi offer to honor the APY they advertised at the time I deposited {$30000.00}, nor did they address the lack of clear disclosure during signup. Instead, they insisted the rate would only apply if I paid a subscription fee or met recurring deposit requirements. 

SoFis advertising ( Supercharge your savings and earn up to 4.30 % APY, Earn up to 4.30 % APY ) did not clearly disclose these paywalled conditions. The APY terms are only shown in fine print ( Earn up to 4.30 % APY on XXXX XXXX with a 0.70 % APY Boost Open a new SoFi Checking & Savings account and enroll in SoFi XX/XX/XXXX Rates variable, subject to change ), and these terms were not apparent during the signup flow. 

This creates a misleading and deceptive impression that simply opening the account provides access to the advertised APY, when in reality the rate is locked behind ongoing requirements, including paying a subscription fee.

I am withdrawing my funds from SoFi as a result and request that the CFPB review SoFis APY advertising and onboarding disclosures for compliance with federal truth-in-savings and unfair or deceptive practices standards. 

The conduct described above is not only misleading in a common-sense consumer understanding, it also aligns closely with what federal courts and regulators have repeatedly held to be deceptive under the Consumer Financial Protection Act ( XXXX ), the Truth in Savings Act ( XXXX ), and the long-standing FTC Act deception standard incorporated into CFPB enforcement. 

Under XXXX, XXXX XXXX. XXXX, a practice is deceptive if : A representation, omission, or practice is likely to mislead a consumer The consumers interpretation is reasonable under the circumstances The misleading information is material Every part of this standard fits SoFis APY advertising. 

XXXX. Likely to mislead hidden APY conditions courts reject Federal courts have consistently held that financial advertisements are deceptive when the headline promise is contradicted by buried or unclear conditions. 
Examples include : FTC v. XXXX, XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXXXX/XX/XXXXXXXX ) XX/XX/XXXXXXXX XXXX held a marketing claim deceptive because the " net impression '' of the offer misled consumerseven though technical conditions existed somewhere in the fine print. The court emphasized that what matters is the overall takeaway, not isolated disclaimers. 

CFPB XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX ( XX/XX/XXXX. XXXX ) The court affirmed that financial offers are deceptive when key conditions are buried in secondary text, making consumers reasonably believe a benefit is available when it is not. 

CFPB XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XX/XX/XXXX XXXX ) The deception finding turned on how a company structured its product so consumers were inevitably misled despite the existence of detailed terms elsewhere. 

SoFis use of Earn up to 4.30 % APY in bold, large fonts while burying the SoFi XXXX condition below the fold fits the exact pattern these cases condemn. 

XXXX. Reasonable consumer standard headline APY dominates The CFPB applies a reasonable consumer standard, not a sophisticated financial-professional standard. 

The big bold headline Supercharge your savings and earn up to 4.30 % APY defines the reasonable consumers understanding. 

High Yield Savings Account - Op Courts have repeatedly ruled that : Consumers read headlines, not footnotes Fine-print or Terms apply language does not cure a misleading headline See : FTC XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX ) underlying district court findings emphasized that consumers initial takeaway controls. 

In re XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( FTC ) disclaimers can not take back the promise made upfront. 

A reasonable consumer opening an account after reading earn up to 4.30 % APY would not assume they must pay a subscription fee everyXX/XX/XXXX days to maintain the rate. 

XXXX. Materiality APY is a core financial term APY is XXXX of the most material terms in retail banking. 

Under XXXX ( XXXX XXXX XXXX ) and CFPB official commentary : Interest rate disclosures must be clear and conspicuous at the time of advertising. 

Material conditions affecting APY must be disclosed in close proximity to the APY statement Advertisements may not present a higher APY without immediately and clearly disclosing conditions required to obtain that APY SoFis presentation separates : Headline : Supercharge your savings and earn up to 4.30 % APY Hidden condition : Enroll in SoFi XX/XX/XXXXPay the SoFi XX/XX/XXXX subscription fee every XX/XX/XXXX days These conditions are nowhere near the headline, violating the proximity requirement recognized in XXXX XXXX XXXX ( b ). 

XXXX. The net impression test the nail in the coffin Both the FTC and CFPB rely on the net impression test, reaffirmed in : FTC XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX XXXX. XXXX ) CFPB XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX XX/XX/XXXXXXXX ) CFPB XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XX/XX/XXXXXXXX. XXXX ) Even if all SoFis terms existed somewhere on the page, what matters is the impression created in the consumers mind by the marketing. 

The net impression of the SoFi page is that opening the account allows consumers to earn the 4.30 percent APY. The fact that the rate is actually contingent on : paying a subscription fee or repeatedly hitting deposit rules or maintaining direct deposits changes the substance of the offer. 

Courts uniformly treat this mismatch as deceptive. 

XXXX. Paywalling an APY is itself unusual and material Courts have held that when a financial institution conditions a benefit on non-standard or surprising requirements, those requirements must be clearly and prominently disclosed. 

See : CFPB XXXX XXXX XXXX Bank, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX XXXX XXXX ) undisclosed non-standard conditions on financial benefits were ruled deceptive and unfair. 

A bank requiring a subscription fee to obtain an interest rate is non-standard in retail banking and requires unmistakable disclosure. 

XXXX. Misleading by omission buried conditions are treated as deception The law recognizes deceptive omission when a company fails to disclose material restrictions that would affect a consumers decision. 

This was reaffirmed in : FTC XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX XXXX. XXXX ) CFPB XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XX/XX/XXXXXXXX ) SoFis failure to place its APY conditions clearly alongside the APY statement is an omission that directly impacts a consumers financial decision precisely the type regulators target. 

Conclusion ( for the CFPB reviewer ) SoFis advertising meets every element of a deceptive financial practice under the CFPA, violates the clear and conspicuous requirements of the Truth in Savings Act, and creates a misleading net impression under binding federal case law. Conditioning an advertised APY on a hidden subscription fee or recurring direct-deposit requirements is not standard industry practice and must be disclosed prominently at the point where the APY is advertised.

ECOA requires creditors to provide : A clear, specific reason for the adverse action, A notice of the consumers rights, and Disclosure of the information used in making the decision.

Citi did not provide accurate or complete reasons for the closure, nor did they meaningfully disclose the source of the bankruptcy claim. Vague or pretextual explanationssuch as expiration of card or other generic excusesdo not satisfy ECOA 's requirements for adverse action notices.

3. Dillards card Refused to correct or reinstate the Citi Macys American Express accountthe account with the highest credit limit Failed to correct the cascading harm caused to my accounts with other creditors Although federal consumer-protection laws do not explicitly codify a retaliation statute for credit card issuers, courts and regulators have routinely held that punitive or adverse actions taken in response to a consumer exercising their rights may constitute : Bad-faith conduct Unfair or deceptive practices under the CFPB UDAAP authority ( unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices ) Violations of ECOA, when adverse actions appear to be tied to a consumer exercising a protected right to dispute or challenge information Citis selective reopening of a low-limit account, followed by later closure and ongoing punitive behavior, supports the reasonable inference of retaliatory intent.

4. Unauthorized Inquiry and Continued Mishandling Under FCRA Citi conducted a credit inquiry that I did not authorize. Their responsereclassifying it as a non-display or soft inquirydoes not resolve the issue.

Unprompted closure notice At XXXX XXXX PST on XX/XX/year>, I received a text message from Chase stating they needed additional information from me and that my accounts were in danger of being closed.

He said he could not provide any reason other than that Chase was protecting the financial institution, citing vague references to their Terms of Service.

About my business ( context for CFPB ) : My business has been operating legally for three years. 

It is a registered LLC in the United States. 

It files taxes annually and maintains proper accounting records. 

It operates in the crypto and blockchain sector, which is legal and fully reported for tax purposes. 

Having traditional banking access is necessary because crypto is a single-sided asset, and my business needs cash flow and fiat on-ramps to function. 

Refusal to provide account statements or balances I asked XXXX for copies of my account statements and balances, because I could no longer access my online banking. 

He said he would not and could not provide them. 

He told me to physically visit a branch and ask a bank manager instead. 

This is unreasonable because Chase is the one who initiated the closure and restricted access without warning. 

Funds currently held/ frozen I have approximately {$20000.00} pending between XXXX, XXXX XXXX, and cleared balances in the Chase business account. 

I asked XXXX what would happen to those funds and how I would receive them. 

He said Chase would send me a check at an unspecified time. 

He could not confirm the amount, timing, or whether incoming deposits would still be honored or rejected. 

Impact on my business and livelihood Chases sudden, unexplained closure and refusal to provide documentation prevents me from accessing my own business funds. 

Payments for services I have already performed are now stuck in limbo, creating cash-flow problems. 

This disrupts my business during the holiday period when financial predictability is essential. 

Chase 's actions appear to be discriminatory against lawful crypto-related businesses despite full tax compliance and transparency. 

Chases lack of transparency I requested a specific explanation for the closure, and XXXX explicitly told me he could not provide any reason. 

He said only that it was to protect Chase as an institution. 

The call was recorded on their end, but I was not provided access to the recording. 

No written explanation has been provided. 

What I Am Requesting I am requesting : A clear explanation for why my business and personal accounts are being closed. 

Immediate access to my account statements, full balances, and transaction history, including pending deposits. 

A detailed explanation of how incoming XXXX and XXXX XXXX payments are being handled, including whether they are being accepted, rejected, or held. 

A specific timeline for when and how my funds will be returned. 

Assurance that Chase is not unlawfully or discriminatorily debanking customers who operate legally in the crypto and blockchain sector. 

Restoration of account access and online banking until the closure and transfer of funds is completed with transparency. 

Why This Requires CFPB Intervention I was given zero explanation for account closures. 

Chase refused to provide statements or balances even though they are required to. 

Funds in legitimate business accounts are being withheld with no timeline. 

This action disrupts a lawful, tax-paying small business. 

It appears to be part of a broader pattern of banks debanking crypto-involved businesses without cause. 

Chases behavior directly contradicts consumer protection standards, transparency requirements, and the CFPBs mandates for fair treatment.

This created financial harm I could not anticipate or prevent.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am filing a complaint regarding XXXX  handling of multiple unauthorized XXXX transactions on my account. I did not authorize these transactions.

I submitted a Regulation E unauthorized EFT dispute to XXXX on XXXX, but the credit union denied my claim on the 9th business day, which violates 12 CFR 1005.11. Regulation E requires a financial institution to either ( 1 ) complete the investigation within 10 business days or ( 2 ) issue provisional credit by the 10th business day if more time is needed. XXXX did neither. 

XXXX  denial was based on the claim that a device ID matched and an IP address matched, but under Regulation E this does not prove that I authorized the transactions. Device IDs and IP addresses can be reused, compromised, or accessed without my knowledge. Regulation E requires proof of consumer authorization not assumptions based on technical logs. 

XXXX also told me that because XXXX has not responded with information, the transactions must be authorized.

This is incorrect under Regulation E : merchant non-response does not constitute proof of authorization, and the burden of proof is on the financial institution, not the consumer. 

XXXX also stated that incoming XXXX funds were not disputed, which is irrelevant under Regulation E. Each outgoing transaction must be evaluated individually, and incoming transfers do not make outgoing transfers authorized.

I have repeatedly stated that I did not authorize these XXXX transactions. XXXX has not provided evidence that I performed or benefited from the transfers. Instead, they denied the claim prematurely and without following the required Regulation E procedures.

Subject : Denial of Check Fraud Claim for Altered/Washed Check ( UCC 4-406 Dispute ) I am writing to dispute the denial of my recent fraud claim regarding a {$10000.00} check ( Check # XXXX ) that was stolen, " washed '' ( altered ), and fraudulently cashed from my Chase checking account. 
The denial of this claim is unacceptable. As a long-term, loyal Chase customer with both my mortgage and all banking accounts entrusted to you, I expect a full and immediate reimbursement, as required under the Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ). 
Summary of Facts The following is a clear timeline of the events : 1. XX/XX/XXXX : I mailed my XXXX tax payments from the XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX, GA ) via Certified Mail. 
Check # XXXX ( IRS ) : Tracking # XXXX. This check was successfully delivered on XX/XX/XXXX. 
Check # XXXX ( GA XXXX. of XXXX ) : {$10000.00}. Tracking # XXXX. This envelope was compromised. 
2. XX/XX/XXXX : Check # XXXX, which was made out to the " Georgia Department of Revenue, '' was washed and fraudulently altered to be payable to a " XXXX XXXX '' and was subsequently paid/cashed by XXXX Bank and cleared from my Chase account. 
3. XX/XX/XXXX : Having filed for a tax extension, this was the deadline to finalize my filing. On this day, I was notified by the Georgia Department XXXX XXXX that my {$10000.00} tax payment was never received. 
4. XX/XX/XXXX : On the same day I was notified of the fraud, I took immediate action : I filed a fraud claim with my local Chase Bank branch. 
I filed a mail theft claim with the XXXX XXXX XXXX ( Ref # XXXX ). 
I filed a fraud report with the XXXX XXXX XXXX ( Case # XXXX ). 
5. XX/XX/XXXX : Chase notified me that my claim was denied, citing that I had failed to report the fraud within the XXXX time limit. 
1. Basis for Dispute : Unjust Denial Based on Reporting Timeframe The denial of my claim due to a XXXX reporting limit is misapplication of the rule. Chase 's position is based on the time since the check was cashed ( XX/XX/XXXX ), not the time since the fraud was discoverable by me. 
I am the customer, not a forensic accountant. I had no reason to believe the check was not paid properly, as the funds had left my account. 
I could not have reasonably known about the fraud until the intended payee ( the GA Dept. of XXXX ) notified me of non-payment. 
I reported the fraud to Chase, the XXXX, and the police on the very day of discovery ( XX/XX/XXXX ). My reporting was prompt and immediate. 
To hold a customer responsible for third-party fraud is contrary to the principles of customer protection. 
2. Legal Basis for Reversal of Denial : Liability Under the Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ) As a large, FDIC-insured bank, Chase has a clear legal obligation to protect its customers from check fraud.

Under the UCC, a bank ( the XXXX Bank ) may only charge an item against a customer 's account if it is " properly payable. '' A check that has been " washed '' to alter the payee is the definition of an altered instrument. 
An altered instrument is not properly payable. 
Therefore, Chase ( the XXXX Bank ) is liable to me, the customer, for paying this item and must re-credit my account. Chase did not use ordinary care in paying the {$10000.00} to the fraudulent payee. 
My customer relationship is with Chase. The law dictates that my recourse is with my bank.

Demand for Resolution I have done everything a customer is supposed to do : I used Certified Mail for security, I notified Chase immediately upon discovery of the altered check, and I filed extensive reports with all relevant authorities.

Consumer complaint narrative:
Issue : Chase refused to properly file my unauthorized debit card fraud claim, incorrectly closed it, and refused to provide provisional credit as required under Regulation E. 

What happened : I noticed an unauthorized debit card transaction from XXXX on my Chase account and immediately contacted Chase to report it. I clearly stated that I did not authorize the transaction, I did not use my debit card or PIN at the merchant, and no one else had permission to use my card.

Despite this, Chase refused to process the claim correctly. Multiple representatives told me that because a PIN was used, the claim was automatically denied and could not be reopened. This is incorrect and violates Regulation XXXX A PIN being used does NOT make a transaction authorized, and card/PIN compromise is a well-documented form of fraud. Chase initially refused to investigate, refused to accept my statement of unauthorized use, and refused to issue the required provisional credit. 

I was later told that the claim had been closed without any investigation and without provisional credit, even though I was originally told I would receive provisional credit no later than Monday. I was then informed I would need to provide compelling evidence to prove fraud solely because a PIN was used. This is an improper shifting of the burden of proof onto the consumer. Regulation E requires the bank to investigate an unauthorized electronic fund transfer, not place the burden on the consumer to disprove a PIN transaction. 

Why this violates Regulation E : The bank must accept and investigate a report of an unauthorized EFT ( 12 CFR 1005 ).

The bank may not refuse to open a claim because of a PIN being used. 
The bank must provide provisional credit if it can not resolve the claim within XXXX business days. 
The burden of proof is on the bank to show the transaction was authorized not on the consumer to prove it wasnt. 
Chase closed my claim without proper investigation and refused multiple times to take my report.

Impact : This has caused unnecessary stress and financial harm because Chase refused to follow federal law and repeatedly refused to process my claim properly.
