Their refusal to provide secure, electronic document submission options contravenes the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act ( GLBA ), specifically its Safeguards Rule, which mandates that financial institutions implement reasonable measures to protect sensitive customer information from unauthorized access or misuse. Insisting on mailing or repeatedly ignoring faxed highly sensitive documents like Social Security cards exposes customers to fraud risks, potentially constituting an unfair or deceptive act under the Consumer Financial Protection Act and FTC regulations. This not only fails to safeguard nonpublic personal information but also smacks of predatory tactics that exploit customers ' trust. I financed an XXXX  purchase and installation through a XXXX credit card that was promoted and described to me at XXXX XXXX of sale as an interest free XXXX financing option. The deferred-interest structure and the fact that interest would be applied retroactively to the entire balance if not paid in full by the promotion end date were not explained to me in a way I understood. 

I immediately set up automatic monthly payments with the intention of paying off the balance in full without accruing interest and never missed a payment. Based on how the financing was presented and my consistent autopay activity, I believed I was satisfying my payment and financing obligation. I did not carry a balance to avoid payment and was intentionally paying down the balance every month. 

On XX/XX/year>, after the promotional period ended, Synchrony applied {$5900.00} in retroactive interest to my account. I did not receive a clear, proactive notice explaining that failure to pay the balance in full by the promotion end date would result in all accrued interest being added retroactively or that the promotion end date was approaching, outside of that information being included in monthly statement documents.

I contacted Synchrony immediately after discovering the interest charge to request an explanation and to ask whether a goodwill adjustment or partial interest credit could be considered given my payment history and the misunderstanding of the promotional terms.

Synchrony advised that no adjustment was possible solely because more than 30 days had passed since the promotion ended and stated that customer service and account resolution teams lacked the ability within their system to review or address the matter further. I was not provided with any alternative review or escalation path.

I am not disputing that the charge may be contractually permitted. However, I would not have agreed to this financing arrangement had the deferred-interest terms and the retroactive application been clearly explained to me at the time of sale. I do not recall the term " deferred-interest '' ever being used at the time of sale of subsequently. I have acted in good faith, made consistent payments, and sought resolution immediately upon learning of the issue.

I am requesting that Synchrony review this matter for a one-time goodwill interest adjustment or partial credit in light of the unclear promotional disclosure, my consistent payment history, and the disproportionate financial impact of the retroactive interest charge.

Consumer complaint narrative:
On XX/XX/2025, I arrived at XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, for a vacation that was fully prepaid prior to my arrival. 
During my stay, I was invited to attend a sales presentation on resort property for a 10-year vacation membership. Payment for the membership was made using two American Express credit cards.

The merchant expressly represented, both verbally and in writing, that the agreement included a 5-day rescission ( cancellation ) period. No benefits or services from the membership were ever used, as my stay had already been fully paid prior to execution of the agreement. 
On XX/XX/2025, well within the stated 5-day cancellation period, my spouse and I exercised our right to rescind the agreement. We : Canceled in person at the merchants office prior to checking out of the resort ; Submitted a written cancellation notice in accordance with the merchants instructions; Sent the cancellation notice via certified mail to the merchants main office ; Left physical copies of the cancellation at both the merchants office and the hotel front desk.

The merchant advised that only a minimal administrative/legal processing fee would apply to cover paperwork.

Despite this lawful and timely rescission, the merchant continued to bill recurring monthly charges to my American Express account after cancellation, for services never rendered.

Nature of the Billing Error The disputed charges constitute billing errors under 15 U.S.C. 1666 ( b ) and 12 C.F.R. 1026.13, including : Charges for services not accepted and not delivered as agreed ; Charges incurred after lawful cancellation ; Charges resulting from misrepresentation and deceptive practices.

American Expresss Failures I timely notified American Express of the dispute and provided clear documentary evidence showing : Proper rescission within the contractual cancellation period ; Non-use of any membership services ; Ongoing billing after cancellation.

Nevertheless, American Express refused to reverse the charges, failed to properly classify the dispute as an FCBA billing error, and did not conduct a reasonable investigation as required by Regulation Z.

American Express : Failed to treat post-cancellation billing as unlawful ; Disregarded clear evidence of timely rescission ; Improperly deferred to the merchant despite contradictory documentation ; Required payment of charges not legally owed.

This conduct violates 12 C.F.R. 1026.13 ( e ), which obligates creditors to either correct billing errors or provide a written explanation supported by evidence. American Express failed to do so.

Consumer Harm As a result of American Expresss failure to comply with federal law, I have suffered : Financial harm from unauthorized recurring charges ; Time and expense attempting to resolve the issue ; Loss of statutory protections guaranteed under the FCBA.

I repeatedly informed TD Bank, both in person at a branch and multiple times by phone, that I was the victim of an impersonation and social-engineering scam. I was contacted by an individual who falsely represented themselves as being associated with XXXX. The communications appeared legitimate and included a XXXX-branded email, a spoofed phone number that appeared as XXXX in my caller ID, and follow-up text messages. I was instructed to screen share from my device and was led to believe that the transfers were necessary to resolve an account issue. At no point did I knowingly authorize transfers to a scammer, nor did I believe I was sending funds to an unknown third party.

The fact that a customer may have physically initiated a transaction does not, by itself, establish that the transaction was authorized if the action was induced by deception, impersonation, or misunderstanding. TD Bank did not provide evidence demonstrating that my authorization was informed and voluntary, nor did it explain what specific evidence supported its conclusion.

I disclosed this during the dispute process because I sometimes communicate differently and may require clearer explanations to avoid misunderstandings. TD Bank did not acknowledge this disclosure, did not offer any communication accommodations, and did not explain how it ensured my statements were accurately understood before denying my claims. I am concerned that my communications were misinterpreted and that this contributed to the improper classification of my dispute.

The bank also did not provide documentation or evidence supporting its conclusion that the transfers were authorized beyond general references to XXXX terms. 

I am requesting that TD Bank be required to re-review my claims under Regulation E with proper consideration of impersonation-based fraud, deception, and accessibility obligations. I am also requesting a clear, evidence-based explanation of how TD Bank concluded that these transactions were authorized despite my repeated statements that they resulted from a scam and misunderstanding.

Failed to provide the documents relied upon to deny the dispute.

Consumer Complaint Regarding Suspicious Banking Practices and Irregular Verification Procedures Institution : Goldman Sachs Bank USA XXXX Marcus by Goldman Sachs ) Product Type : Deposit Account / External Account Transfers Summary of Complaint I am filing this complaint to report suspicious and irregular banking practices by Goldman Sachs Bank USA related to external account verification and funds transfers. The bank implemented an unusual and unexplained post-transaction verification process that materially deviates from standard banking practices, contradicts prior confirmations, and created confusion and concern regarding the legitimacy and security of my transaction. 

Detailed Description of the Issue I maintain a Marcus by Goldman Sachs deposit account and have had multiple external bank accounts linked to this account over time. Historically : External accounts were linked through standard online verification procedures. 
Transfers were completed after electronic confirmation. 

At no point was a third, post-transaction telephone verification required to complete or validate transfers. 
This process was consistent with my experience at other financial institutions, liked to my Marcus accounts, including XXXX XXXX, which I recently closed and which never required such verification at Goldman Sachs.

Recently, I added a new external bank account to my Marcus account. The process unfolded as follows : I completed the external account linking and verification process through Goldman Sachs online system.

I received electronic confirmation that the external account was successfully linked.

I initiated a transfer from the newly linked external account. 

I received confirmationboth online and via emailthat the transfer was successfully processed. 
Despite these confirmations, three days later, Goldman Sachs Bank USA contacted me after normal business hours ( approximately XXXX XXXX. ), stating that they needed to complete an additional verification by phone with the external bank in order to finalize the transfer. 

This request by phone was highly irregular for the following reasons : The account had already been verified and linked. 
The transfer had already been confirmed as completed. 
No prior disclosure indicated that a secondary, post-confirmation phone verification would be required. 

This verification requirement was inconsistent with industry norms and my prior banking experience. 
The timing and nature of the call raised concerns about the legitimacy of the request and whether the transaction was being improperly delayed or interfered with. 
Consumer Concerns Goldman Sachs Bank USAs actions raise several serious concerns, including : Lack of transparency regarding verification requirements, Potential unfair or deceptive practices by confirming transactions and later imposing undisclosed conditions Inconsistent application of security procedures, Risk of consumer confusion and exposure to fraud, as the call resembled tactics commonly associated with financial scams, and Unwarranted delays or interference with lawful access to funds. 

At no point prior to or during the transaction was I informed that a post-confirmation telephone verification would be required. Had I received such a call from any other source, it would reasonably be interpreted as fraudulent.

Harm and Impact : As a result of Goldman Sachs Bank USAs actions : I experienced confusion and concern regarding the security of my account. 
I was placed in a position where complying with the request could expose me to fraud. 
My confidence in the institutions internal controls and consumer safeguards has been undermined.

My access to funds was placed at risk after confirmation had already been provided.

Requested Resolution : I respectfully request that the CFPB and FDIC : Review Goldman Sachs Bank USAs external account verification and transfer practices. 
Determine whether post-confirmation verification requirements were properly disclosed and compliant with applicable consumer protection laws. 
Require Goldman Sachs Bank USA to provide a written explanation of : Why the transfer was confirmed and later subjected to additional verification Why the verification occurred days later and after business hours Whether this practice is applied uniformly to all consumers Ensure that Goldman Sachs Bank USA implements clear, consistent, and transparent procedures that do not expose consumers to fraud risk or unfair delays. 
I am submitting this complaint in good faith to protect my financial interests and to prevent similar issues from affecting other consumers.

I am filing this complaint regarding an unauthorized ATM withdrawal of {$680.00} from my Cash App account on XX/XX/year>, at a XXXX XXXX  ATM. 

I did not authorize this transaction. My Cash App card was in my possession at the time, and I did not knowingly share my PIN. This withdrawal occurred due to an unauthorized PIN compromise, which I did not discover until after the transaction posted. 

Cash App denied my dispute solely on the basis that the transaction was completed using the card and PIN and that my account showed other activity earlier that day. This determination is flawed and does not meet the requirements of Regulation E ( 12 CFR 1005 ). 

The presence of prior legitimate transactions does not establish authorization of a later fraudulent ATM withdrawal. Additionally, PIN compromise can occur without card loss or intentional disclosure, and delayed discovery of fraud is explicitly recognized under Regulation E. 

The transaction history on this date shows indicators of fraud, including multiple balance inquiries prior to the ATM withdrawal, which is a known fraud pattern. Cash App did not investigate these indicators, did not request or review ATM camera footage, and did not meaningfully assess whether the withdrawal was truly authorized. 

Cash App has refused to allow a further appeal and has closed its internal dispute process, leaving no consumer remedy. 

I am requesting that this matter be escalated for a full Regulation Ecompliant review and that the unauthorized {$680.00} ATM withdrawal be provisionally and permanently credited back to my account.

Subject : Apple Card account closure ( XX/XX/year> ) adverse action without specific reasons ( ECOA / Regulation B ), full credit reporting disclosures, specific contractual basis, and account history relied upon I am submitting this complaint regarding the closure of an Apple Card account issued by Goldman Sachs Bank USA, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. 

The Apple Card account at issue was closed effective XX/XX/year>. At the time of closure, the account was in good standing. The remaining balance has since been paid in full, and the current balance is {$0.00}, as confirmed by Apple Card Support. 

The account closure notice stated that the account was closed because there was a failure to comply with the terms of the Customer Agreement. No further explanation was provided identifying which specific provision of the Customer Agreement was allegedly violated, what conduct formed the basis of this determination, or what account data was relied upon.

I contend that the closure of this Apple Card account constitutes an adverse action under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act ( ECOA ). Under 15 U.S.C. 1691 ( d ) ( 2 ) and its implementing regulation, 12 C.F.R. 1002.9 ( b ) ( 2 ) ( Regulation B ), a creditor that takes an adverse action is required to provide a statement of reasons that is specific and that indicates the principal reason ( s ) for the adverse action. A generic statement that the customer failed to comply with the terms of the Customer Agreement, without identifying any specific term, conduct, or factual basis, does not satisfy this statutory and regulatory requirement.

In addition, pursuant to the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), including 15 U.S.C. 1681m ( a ) and 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2, I am entitled to know whether any consumer report was obtained or used in connection with this adverse action and to receive confirmation that any information furnished to consumer reporting agencies is complete and accurate.

Since the account closure, I have contacted Apple Card Support multiple times via XXXX and telephone, requesting clarification and compliance with these legal requirements. Apple Card Support responded, among other times, on XX/XX/XXXX, XXXX days after the account closureand again on XX/XX/year>, each time reiterating only generic contractual language stating that the issuer reserves the right to close an account at any time, with or without notice. None of these responses identified a specific contractual provision, factual basis, adverse action analysis, credit reporting details, or the account history relied upon. 

I am not disputing Goldman Sachs Bank USAs contractual right to close an account. Rather, I am requesting confirmation that Goldman Sachs Bank USA has complied with its statutory obligations under ECOA and FCRA. 

Specifically, I request that Goldman Sachs Bank USA provide : 1. Confirmation that the closure of the Apple Card account on XX/XX/year> was treated as an adverse action under ECOA, or a clear explanation of why it was not.

2. A specific statement of reasons, as required by 15 U.S.C. 1691 ( d ) ( 2 ) and 12 C.F.R. 1002.9 ( b ) ( 2 ), identifying the principal reason ( s ) for the account closure, including the specific provision ( s ) of the Customer Agreement allegedly violated. 
3. Identification of the specific account history, activity, or data relied upon in determining that the Customer Agreement was violated, including, at a minimum, the category or type of account activity ( for example, types of transactions, use patterns, or other account data ), even if individual transaction-level details are not provided.

4. Confirmation of whether any consumer report or information from any consumer reporting agency was obtained, reviewed, or relied upon in connection with the decision to close the account. 
5. Full disclosure of all information furnished to any consumer reporting agency, whether positive or negative, including account status, remarks, codes, comments, payment history, or classifications, and confirmation that the account is accurately reported as closed by the creditor, with no derogatory notations.

6. Confirmation of whether any adverse action notice or additional disclosure was required or provided under ECOA and/or FCRA, and if not, the legal basis for that determination.

I am requesting the CFPBs assistance in ensuring that Goldman Sachs Bank USA provides the disclosures and specificity required by law. I am seeking clarification and compliance only and am not requesting reinstatement of the account, monetary compensation, or enforcement action.

This shifts the 30 % calculation from the transaction amount ( as stated in the headline ) to the rewards earnings. This changes the offer from a massive additive bonus ( e.g., 1 % + 30 % = 31 % return ) to a negligible multiplicative bonus ( e.g., 1 % x 1.3 = 1.3 % return ). 


3. Materiality and Injury ( Financial Damages ) This deception was material to my decision-making and directly altered my financial behavior in three specific ways : Lost Opportunity Cost : I charged {$700.00} to this card instead of my alternative card which earns a guaranteed 7 % cash back. Induced Spending : I made {$990.00} in discretionary purchases solely because I believed I was receiving a 31 % discount. I would not have made these purchases otherwise. 
Behavioral Manipulation : The offer required spending " at least {$1500.00} '' and making " at least 10 qualifying purchases ''. My historical average with this card is roughly 7 transactions totaling less than XXXX XXXXXXXX. Because of this deceptive offer, I spent over {$2500.00} this montha 400 % increase over my normal usagespecifically to meet the thresholds advertised. 


4. Timing of Disclosure The promotional banner appeared approximately two weeks prior to the clarifying email received on XX/XX/year>. b'Capital One XXXX Credit Card# XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXAmount in Dispute:  $XXXX  NATURE OF COMPLAINT

On XXXX XXXX XXXX I discovered that five previously authorized ACH credit card payments made to my Capital One account are being reversed through "R10" return codes--"Customer Advises Not Authorized"--initiated by XXXX XXXX, (acting as the Receiving Depository Financial Institution ("RDFI") for XXXX XXXX XXXX account). These reversals are improper because: (1) I never claimed these transactions were unauthorized; (2) I never signed or provided a Written Statement of Unauthorized Debit ("WSUD") as mandatorily required under NACHA Operating Rules; and (3) XXXX  is abusing the "R10" code to cover an overdraft in a separate, unrelated account (XXXX XXXX).

Capital One, as the Originating Depository Financial Institution ("ODFI"), has the right and responsibility under NACHA Rules to dishonor these improperly initiated returns. If Capital One allows these returns to process without exercising its rights under the NACHA Operating Rules, I will be liable for double payment on my credit card account--a result that is both unjust and contrary to the consumer protection purposes of the ACH system.

II. FACTUAL BACKGROUND

A. The Authorized Transactions

I maintain a XXXX XXXX XXXX account held at XXXX XXXX. Using this account, I made the following authorized ACH payments to my Capital One credit card:

 XXXX XXXX XXXX $XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX $XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX $XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX: $XXXXThese transactions were properly authorized by me, processed through the ACH network, and credited to my Capital One credit card account. I have no dispute regarding these transactions.

B. The Improper "R10" Returns

On XXXX XXXX XXXX I discovered five pending transactions on my Capital One credit card account labeled "Returned Mobile ACH Payment -- CONA" totaling $XXXX Capital One customer service informed me that XXXX XXXX  returned these transactions using "R10" return codes with the notation "Customer Advises Not Authorized."

This is false. I never advised XXXX  or any other party that these transactions were unauthorized. I never signed, submitted, or provided any Written Statement of Unauthorized Debit. XXXX has fabricated or misrepresented the basis for these returns.

C. The True Reason for XXXX  Actions

There is a separate XXXX account that went into overdraft as of approximately XXXX XXXX XXXX due to unrelated transactions. Prior to that overdraft, I had transferred funds from that account into my Cash Plus account (the account used to make the Capital One payments). Rather than pursuing proper collection remedies for the overdraft in the separate account, XXXX  is abusing the ACH "R10" return code system to claw back funds from Capital One--funds that were properly paid from my Cash Plus account, which was never in overdraft.

This is an improper use of the "R10" code, which exists solely to address genuinely unauthorized transactions upon a customer's signed, sworn statement--not as a collection mechanism for unrelated account overdrafts.

III. NACHA RULE VIOLATIONS

A. XXXX Breach of Warranty (Subsection 3.13.2)

Under the NACHA Operating Rules, an RDFI transmitting an "R10" Extended Return Entry makes a specific warranty to the ODFI. Subsection 3.13.2 states:

"An RDFI that Transmits an Extended Return Entry warrants to each ODFI, ACH Operator, and Gateway that, prior to initiating the Extended Return Entry, the RDFI obtained a Written Statement of Unauthorized Debit from the Receiver that conforms to the requirements of Subsection 3.12.4"
\XXXX has warranted to Capital One that it possesses a WSUD signed by me for each of these five transactions. This warranty is false. I never signed any such document. XXXX cannot produce a WSUD because none exists.

B. The Mandatory WSUD Requirement (Subsection 3.12.4)

The NACHA Rules are explicit that the WSUD is mandatory, not optional. Subsection 3.12.4 requires:

"A Written Statement of Unauthorized Debit must be signed or similarly authenticated by the Receiver

The WSUD must include:

 Receiver's printed name and signature

 Receiver's account number

 The identity of the party debiting the account

 The date the entry was posted

 The dollar amount of the entry

 The reason for the return

 An assertion from the Receiver that the WSUD is true and correct

 An assertion that the Receiver is an authorized signer

Without a conforming WSUD, there is no evidence linking the "R10" return to any customer action. The "R10" code is merely an administrative tool for inter-bank communication; it has no probative value regarding whether a customer actually authorized a return.

IV. CAPITAL ONE's RIGHTS AND RESPONSIBILITIES AS ODFI

A. Right to Dishonor the Return (Subsection 2.13.6)

Capital One, as the ODFI, has the right to dishonor these Extended Return Entries. Under NACHA Subsection 2.13.6.1(b), an ODFI may dishonor a return when the RDFI has not complied with the requirements of the NACHA Rules--including the mandatory WSUD requirement.

The NACHA Rules provide Capital One with a Timely Dishonor remedy: Capital One may dishonor the return within 5 banking days of receipt.

B. Right to Demand the WSUD (Subsection 3.12.6)

Capital One has an absolute and unconditional right to demand the WSUD from XXXX. Subsection 3.12.6 states:

"An RDFI Transmitting an Extended Return Entry... must provide to an ODFI a copy of the Written Statement of Unauthorized Debit obtained from the Receiver... within ten Banking Days after receiving a written request from the ODFI

If XXXX fails to provide a conforming WSUD upon Capital One's written request, XXXX will be in breach of its warranty under Subsection 3.13.2, and Capital One may pursue a Late Dishonor or NACHA arbitration.

C. Capital One's Responsibility to Its Customer

If Capital One allows these returns to process without exercising its rights under the NACHA Rules, I will be liable for the original credit card charges plus forced to make replacement payments--effectively paying twice for the same obligations. This outcome:

 Rewards XXXX abuse of the ACH system

 Harms Capital One's customer (me) through no fault of my own

 Undermines the integrity of the ACH network's consumer protections

V. RELIEF REQUESTED

I respectfully request that Capital One:

1. Immediately exercise its right to Dishonor the five pending "R10"  Customer Advises Not Authorized  returns totaling XXXX2. Issue a written request to XXXX XXXX under Subsection 3.12.6 demanding production of the WSUDs purportedly supporting these returns;

3. If XXXX fails to produce conforming WSUDs, pursue all available remedies under NACHA Rules including Late Dishonor and arbitration;

4. Ensure that I am not held liable for double payment as a result of XXXX XXXXmproper conduct.

VI. URGENCY

These reversals are currently pending and processing as of XXXX XXXX XXXX The NACHA Rules provide Capital One with only 5 banking days to exercise a Timely Dishonor. Immediate action is required to prevent irreparable harm to my account and to preserve Capital One's remedies under the NACHA Rules.

Respectfully submitted,

Complaint Narrative I am filing this complaint regarding American Expresss failure to comply with its obligations under the Fair Credit Billing Act and Regulation Z in the handling of billing disputes and the issuance of credits for invalid charges. 
I disputed XXXX charges that were installments of a larger transaction for services that were not provided as promised. I submitted documentation supporting my claim, including a written rebuttal to the merchants response with screenshots showing what actually occurred. The merchant did not submit evidence that negated my claim. American Express credited XXXX installment but denied the other, which further indicates that the dispute handling was not based on a consistent or reasonable evaluation of the evidence.

American Express later refused to reopen the dispute, despite previously stating in writing that the investigation could be reopened if additional documentation indicating a potential change in outcome was provided. I submitted additional documentation and contacted American Express within that timeframe.

On subsequent recorded calls, American Express representatives made statements indicating that dispute outcomes were predetermined and that customer-submitted documentation would not be meaningfully reviewed. On

one recorded call, a representative stated that American Express didnt really look into many disputes, especially the small ones, which were described as transactions of {$25.00} or less, explaining that such disputes are written off because when a customer files a claim, the bank costs {$25.00} to investigate. When I asked whether I could re-upload documentation supporting my dispute, a representative stated there was no
point in submitting additional evidence. Representatives further stated that the dispute could not be reopened because it had been reopened too many times. However, this refusal was not based on a completed, evidence-based investigation. Instead, representatives stated that reopening the claim again would result in the same outcome regardless of any additional documentation.

During a recorded call, an American Express representative explicitly confirmed that even if American Express determined the charge was invalid, it would not issue a credit, explaining that American Express can not make the merchant pay.

This position directly contradicts Regulation Z, which requires an issuer to conduct a reasonable investigation and to credit the consumers account if a charge is found invalid, regardless of whether the merchant reimburses the issuer.

Contradictory Written Representations American Expresss refusal to reopen the dispute contradicts its own prior written communication, in which it stated : If you further question the charge and in case you have documentation indicating that a change in the outcome, please contact us within 30 days and we will be glad to reopen the investigation for you.

Despite submitting additional documentation and contacting American Express within this timeframe, representatives later stated that the claim could not be reopened and that the outcome would not change regardless of evidence. These contradictory statements demonstrate a failure to conduct a reasonable investigation and raise concerns regarding deceptive or unfair practices.

Systemic Compliance Concerns This issue appears to be systemic rather than isolated. On multiple occasions, American Express representatives provided statements that contradict federal law, including : That small-dollar disputes are not meaningfully reviewed because investigation costs exceed the transaction amount ; That a consumer refund depends on whether the merchant reimburses American Express ; and That dispute outcomes are predetermined and would not change even with additional evidence.

These statements indicate a failure to conduct reasonable investigations as required by Regulation Z and suggest internal policies or training that are non-compliant with federal consumer prot

ection law. Account Closure After Escalation My accounts were closed following a period of dispute activity related to the charges described above. After the accounts were closed, I contacted American Express to ask why the closures occurred. Initially, representatives stated they could not provide an explanation. On a subsequent recorded call, an American Express representative explained, in substance, that the accounts were closed due to the volume and nature of disputes I had filed, including what were described as small-dollar disputes, and referenced the cost to American Express of investigating such disputes. The accounts were therefore closed after dispute activity and discussions regarding dispute volume, and before I raised formal compliance concerns with American Express executive leadership. This sequence raises serious concerns regarding the treatment of good-faith dispute activity and whether account-closure decisions were influenced by cost-based or non-compliant dispute handling practices.

Consumer complaint narrative:
PNC bank sent me a promotional circular stating I would get {$200.00} as a reward for using their card. I did so and then they refused to pay me the reward stating I did not qualify for the reward and they knew before hand that I did not qualify for the reward. They engaged in deceptive practice by offering me a reward knowing that I would not qualify for such a reward. 

Note that I believe that they are in violation of one or more items in Michigans code MCL section 445.903 to wit ( a ) Causing a probability of confusion or misunderstanding as to the source, sponsorship, approval, or certification of goods or services.

( c ) Representing that goods or services have sponsorship, approval, characteristics, ingredients, uses, benefits, or quantities that they do not have or that a person has sponsorship, approval, status, affiliation, or connection that he or she does not have. 
( n ) Causing a probability of confusion or of misunderstanding as to the legal rights, obligations, or remedies of a party to a transaction.

( o ) Causing a probability of confusion or of misunderstanding as to the terms or conditions of credit if credit is extended in a transaction.

( q ) Representing or implying that the subject of a consumer transaction will be provided promptly, or at a specified time, or within a reasonable time, if the merchant knows or has reason to know it will not be so provided. 
( r ) Representing that a consumer will receive goods or services free or without charge, or using words of similar import in the representation, without clearly and conspicuously disclosing with equal prominence in immediate conjunction with the use of those words the conditions, terms, or prerequisites to the use or retention of the goods or services advertised. 
( s ) Failing to reveal a material fact, the omission of which tends to mislead or deceive the consumer, and which fact could not reasonably be known by the consumer.

( t ) Entering into a consumer transaction in which the consumer waives or purports to waive a right, benefit, or immunity provided by law, unless the waiver is clearly stated and the consumer has specifically consented to it. 
( v ) Taking or arranging for the consumer to sign an acknowledgment, certificate, or other writing affirming acceptance, delivery, compliance with a requirement of law, or other performance, if the merchant knows or has reason to know that the statement is not true. 
( w ) Representing that a consumer will receive a rebate, discount, or other benefit as an inducement for entering into a transaction, if the benefit is contingent on an event to occur subsequent to the consummation of the transaction. 
( x ) Taking advantage of the consumer 's inability reasonably to protect his or her interests by reason of XXXX, illiteracy, or inability to understand the language of an agreement presented by the other party to the transaction who knows or reasonably should know of the consumer 's inability. 
( bb ) Making a representation of fact or statement of fact material to the transaction such that a person reasonably believes the represented or suggested state of affairs to be other than it actually is. 
( cc ) Failing to reveal facts that are material to the transaction in light of representations of fact made in a positive manner.

Issue : Unauthorized electronic check transaction, account takeover activity, contradictory investigation findings, and failure to credit returned funds Desired Resolution : Credit of funds, lost interest, and written accounting Complaint Description I am filing this complaint regarding PNC Banks failure to resolve an unauthorized electronic check ( e-check ) transaction that occurred as part of an account takeover, and its failure to credit funds that were returned to PNC more than 30 days ago. 
This issue was reported to PNC nearly 60 days ago. 
In early XXXX, my account was accessed without authorization. PNC access activity and transaction history show a pattern consistent with account takeover, including : Unauthorized logins Internal transfers from savings to checking on XX/XX/year> Creation of an unauthorized ACH transaction on XX/XX/year> Repetition of this process XXXX additional times Escalation to a bill-pay check Addition of multiple new bill-pay payees for future processing These actions were not performed by me. 
During multiple phone calls with PNCs fraud department, multiple representatives independently stated that they observed account logins originating from Texas and California, which were inconsistent with my location and travel history. I specifically called back multiple times to confirm that these representatives were not mistaken, and each time I was told the same information. 
However, the completed dispute documentation later provided by PNC states that only familiar logins were observed. This conclusion directly contradicts the representations made by multiple members of PNCs fraud department earlier in the investigation. PNC has not explained this discrepancy or reconciled the conflicting information. 
Despite this documented activity, Executive Client Relations representative XXXX ( works for XXXX XXXX ) stated with 100 % certainty that my identity was not stolen. This determination conflicts with the access activity, transaction sequence, and earlier fraud department statements. 
An Affidavit of Forgery was submitted to PNC approximately 30 days ago. 
The originating institution has confirmed that the funds from the unauthorized e-check were returned to PNC or a PNC-affiliated clearing account more than 30 days ago. My account has not been credited, and PNC has not provided documentation showing where the returned funds were applied.

This matter has been under review by PNC Executive Client Relations for over 30 days. Multiple requests for written status updates and documentation have gone unanswered by Executive Client Relations representatives XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, and XXXX. Local PNC branch representatives have also been unable to assist or provide explanations. 
Additionally, each dispute related to the unauthorized e-check was processed using a different and incorrect account number, which I reported multiple times without response. Any investigation based on incorrect account information is inherently unreliable. 
PNC may attempt to classify this transaction as outside Regulation E. Regardless of classification, the following facts are undisputed : The transaction was unauthorized An Affidavit of Forgery was submitted PNCs own personnel provided conflicting accounts of login activity The funds were recovered and returned to PNC or a PNC-controlled clearing destination PNC has retained the returned funds for over 30 days without crediting my account PNC has failed to provide a written accounting of the returned funds PNCs investigation relied on incorrect account information PNCs failure to credit returned funds or provide a clear accounting constitutes improper handling of an unauthorized transaction and a failure to resolve an error, whether analyzed under Regulation E, the Check 21 Act, or UCC Articles 3 and 4.

As a result of PNCs prolonged failure to resolve this matter, I have lost interest on the funds during the period PNC has retained them and have experienced ongoing financial harm.

Requested Resolution I am requesting that PNC : 1. Immediately credit my account for the full amount of the unauthorized e-check 2. Pay lost interest for the period the funds were retained by PNC 3. Provide written documentation showing the return path and final disposition of the funds 4. Reconcile and explain the contradictory fraud investigation findings 5. Correct the dispute record and close the matter with a written explanation 6. Provide written confirmation that the transactions were determined to be unauthorized, that I bear no liability for them, and that no adverse reporting, account abuse designation, or negative internal or external reporting has been or will be made as a result of this incident.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am filing this complaint due to Chimes failure to comply with Regulation E ( 12 C.F.R. Part 1005 ) regarding an unauthorized electronic fund transfer. 

On XX/XX/year>, funds were withdrawn from my account as part of a fraudulent transaction involving a fake merchant website. The merchant provided a fake tracking number and a fake tracking page, and no goods were ever delivered. 

I filed a fraud dispute with Chime on XX/XX/year>. 

Despite this being a fraud-induced transaction, Chime classified the transfer as authorized solely because I entered my payment information, which is inconsistent with CFPB guidance stating that fraud-induced authorization does not constitute actual authorization under Regulation E.

Additionally, Chime failed to issue a provisional credit within 10 business days, and failed to provide written notice that additional time was needed, as required by Regulation E.

Chime also failed to conduct or document a reasonable investigation and did not provide a written explanation of its findings or my rights under Regulation E.

As of today, Chime has not complied with Regulation Es requirements regarding : Provisional credit Timely investigation Proper classification of fraud-induced transfers Written explanation of findings I am requesting that the CFPB require Chime to : 1. Conduct a lawful Regulation E investigation 2. Issue the required provisional credit 3. Correct its misclassification of fraud-induced transactions 4. Provide written findings and documentation as required by law

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am filing this complaint regarding how my credit card issuer handled a dispute involving merchandise not as described, improper merchant fees, and an unauthorized rebilling. 

XXXX and facts : I placed an online order with XXXX for an automotive part advertised and invoiced as an adjuster assembly that includes motor, supported by product images showing a full motor and XXXX XXXX. The amount charged was approximately {$80.00}. 

When the order arrived, the item shipped was not the advertised product. Instead of a XXXX XXXX, I received only a small wiring pigtail ( two wires and a connector ). The item was materially different and unusable. 

I immediately contacted the merchant and provided photos showing the mismatch between what was advertised and what was delivered. 

The merchant acknowledged the return request but required that I pay return shipping and a 20 % restocking fee, despite this being a merchant fulfillment error. 

I disputed the charge with my credit card issuer and submitted all documentation, including : The receipt and product description showing includes motor Photos of the incorrect item received Email correspondence where the merchant demanded shipping costs and a restocking fee The disputed charge was initially removed. 

After the dispute, the merchant re-charged my card without authorization, even though I did not place a new order or approve a rebill. 

I reported this as an unauthorized transaction. My card issuer informed me that they would not take further action unless I returned the incorrect item at my own expense. 

I escalated to a supervisor and explained that this was merchant misrepresentation and an unauthorized rebill, not a buyer-initiated return. Despite this, I was told I must pay return shipping to proceed. 

Issue with the credit card issuer : The credit card issuer is conditioning relief on compliance with the merchants return policy, despite documented evidence that : The merchant shipped materially different goods The merchant attempted to impose improper fees for its own error The merchant re-billed my card without authorization after a dispute I am concerned that my credit card issuer failed to properly investigate the unauthorized rebilling and is improperly shifting financial responsibility to me for merchant misconduct. 

I am requesting that this matter be reviewed to determine whether the credit card issuer appropriately applied dispute and fraud protections and whether requiring the consumer to pay return shipping and fees in this situation is consistent with consumer protection obligations.

XXXX conclusion that I am responsible for this account is unsupported by competent evidence and reflects a legally deficient investigation in violation of federal law. 

Failure to Conduct a Reasonable Investigation Under 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( b ), furnishers of information are required to conduct a reasonable and good-faith investigation upon receipt of notice of a dispute. Courts have repeatedly held that a furnisher may not satisfy this obligation by merely relying on information supplied by a third party or by reviewing internal records alone. 

XXXX v. XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX Cir. XXXX ) ( holding that a furnishers investigation must be reasonable and that merely confirming information from internal databases is insufficient ). 

XXXX v. XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX, XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX Cir. XXXX ) ( a furnisher must conduct a genuine investigation and can not simply parrot information received from the original creditor ). 

XXXX v. XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX Cir. XXXX ) ( finding that reliance on a creditors representations without independent verification may constitute an unreasonable investigation ). 

XXXX response demonstrates precisely the conduct rejected in these decisionsuncritical reliance on documents provided by XXXX, a third party with a direct financial interest in validating the transaction. 

Lack of Proof of Authorization Assertions regarding account logins, email communications, or alleged installation of equipment do not establish contractual liability or authorization. Federal courts have made clear that documentation generated after account opening or tied only to an address or email is insufficient to prove identity or consent. 

XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX Md. XXXX XXXX, XXXX ) ( finding that billing statements and account activity do not establish that the consumer opened or authorized the account ). 

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX Cir. XXXX ) ( recognizing that inaccurate attribution of debt to a consumer can support FCRA liability when reasonable procedures are lacking ). 

XXXX has produced no contemporaneous evidence showing lawful identity verification at account origination, such as government-issued ID validation, authenticated electronic signatures, IP or device metadata tied to me, or recorded consent. 

Willful and Reckless Noncompliance Where a furnisher continues to report disputed information without adequate verification, courts have found such conduct may constitute willful noncompliance under the FCRA. 

XXXX XXXX. XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX ) ( defining willfulness under the FCRA to include reckless disregard of statutory duties ). 

XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX ( XXXX Cir. XXXX ) ( emphasizing that furnishers and CRAs must do more than make superficial investigations ). 

Formal Demands Accordingly, I hereby demand : An immediate reinvestigation conducted by XXXX  in compliance with 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( b ), independent of XXXX. 

Production of all identity-verification and underwriting records relied upon at account origination, including application metadata, IP logs, device fingerprints, signature authentication records, and internal verification notes. 

Identification of the specific identity-verification and Red Flags compliance procedures XXXX claims to have followed prior to extending credit. 

Written confirmation that the account will remain marked as disputed with all consumer reporting agencies and that no adverse reporting or collection activity will occur during the pendency of this dispute. 

If XXXX continues to assert liability without producing competent proof of authorization, such conduct will be viewed as willful and reckless disregard of its obligations under 15 U.S.C. 1681n and 1681o, exposing XXXX to statutory damages, actual damages, punitive damages, attorneys fees, and costs.

This letter constitutes formal notice and a good-faith opportunity to cure. I reserve all rights and remedies at law and in equity and do not waive any claims by virtue of this correspondence.

Consumer complaint narrative:
Portfolio Recovery Associates states that it purchased an account originally issued by XXXX XXXX XXXX and claims that no further contract was required between PRA and me. This statement is misleading and does not satisfy federal consumer protection requirements. While PRA alleges ownership of an account, it has failed to provide any documentation showing that I personally authorized PRA to access, store, or report my personal information or that I consented to the transfer of my data to PRA. 

The response relies on internal records and statements from the seller and claims that consumer permission or consent is not required to furnish information to consumer reporting agencies. This position conflicts with the Fair Credit Reporting Act. Under 15 USC 1681b, a company must have a permissible purpose to furnish or obtain consumer report information. That permissible purpose must be tied to a lawful relationship or consumer authorization. PRA has not produced any document bearing my signature or consent authorizing PRA to possess or use my personal information. 

PRA also references Privacy Regulation V and its own privacy policy as justification for reporting. A company privacy policy does not override federal law and does not substitute for consumer consent. The absence of an opt out requirement does not eliminate the obligation to demonstrate lawful authority to collect or report. PRA has not shown any agreement that establishes a direct relationship between me and PRA. 

Additionally, PRA asserts that it sent an initial notification letter and that no dispute was received. That claim does not establish lawful authority and does not cure the absence of consumer authorization. Reporting disputed information without verifying the legal basis for data possession violates 15 USC 1681e ( b ), which requires reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy. Accuracy includes legal accuracy and authority to report, not just numerical balances.

The withdrawn amount was a scheduled auto loan payment, but my payment had been formally deferred, as documented by a 90-day extension form issued by the bank, which clearly stated that my next payment was not due until XX/XX/XXXX. 

Despite this, the bank withdrew funds prior to the authorized due date, without my consent or approval. I immediately contacted customer service and a supervisor to dispute this unauthorized withdrawal, providing evidence of the deferment and stating that I never authorized automatic payments.

They directed me to contact the collections department, which has no legal authority to process a dispute for an early withdrawal from my deposit account.

The banks refusal to investigate or reverse the transaction has caused immediate financial harm, as part of the withdrawn funds belonged to a third party ( my roommate ) for rent obligations, and the premature withdrawal prevented me from accessing those funds.

I am formally requesting an investigation and reversal of the unauthorized debit, along with provisional credit while the investigation is completed.

Consumer complaint narrative:
We were the victims of check and debit fraud. We have had someone who has been cleaning our house for over 8 years and unfortunately she stole our checkbook from our house and presumably was able to take a picture of one of our debit cards. It is unclear how or when she stole the checking book since she has been cleaning for us for so long. She also stole a stamp that was used to stamp this belongs to " first name last name '' with purple lettering. Over the summer she started writing fraudulent checks and forged one signature then signed the rest with the stamp she stole. Both our bank and the bank where these checks were deposited were PNC Bank. These were cashed using the mobile deposit functionality where no checks on information, date or signature were performed. In addition at least one of the checks was dated well over 6 months from the date it was deposited. The first fraudulent check was deposited on XX/XX/XXXX. We typically only write XXXX checks per year. We keep track of our balance regularly but unfortunately did not notice that many fraudulent checks were written and deposited over the summer. A total of XXXX checks were cashed between XX/XX/XXXX and XX/XX/XXXX. We get alerts about other potential fraud but received zero alerts about the clearly abnormal and alarming pattern of checks being written. We did not realize this was going on until XX/XX/XXXX and reported it immediately. We have a joint account and my wife happened to be out of the country when we found out. I went to the bank the same day to report the fraud and in discussions with the bank it was decided to put our account on high alert until my wife was able to get home to transfer all our money to a new account. During this time the same person started sending money from one of our debit cards via XXXX. At the time this happened we did not know she had our debit card information as we still had the physical card still. This was realized within XXXX hours of it happening and was reported immediately. In total the amount stolen was {$15000.00}. 

We disputed all of the checks and all of the debit card transactions right away. We were reimbursed one of the 26 checks which was only {$800.00} of the approx {$15000.00}. PNC bank has temporarily given us back the debit fraud amount but these are still listed as " pending dispute '' totaling {$1600.00}. The remaining amount was checks and we were informed a few weeks ago that PNC Bank denied all the remains check disputes arguing that we did not report it in a timely manner. This was of course all reported to the police immediately and we filed charges. This is still an active investigation. 

Personally, I believe that PNC Bank was negligent. Both our account and the fraudulent account were PNC Bank. The PNC Bank app was used to deposit the checks to the fraudulent checks. There was no validation on the checks that were mobile deposited and it was clear by anyone who looked at the check that a stamp was used to sign the checks. There was also a check that was deposited that was dated beyond 6 months. It was also negligent that the bank did not red flag these transactions. We normally use XXXX checks a year and multiple were being written for the same day let alone XXXX over the span of 2 months all to the same person. This 100 % would not have happened if these were attempted to be cashed in person and the fact that PNC Bank is not taking any ownership of this is disappointing. Even the PNC staff who I interacted with had comments of " Oh wow this is clearly fraudulent, '' " Wow you never write checks, this is clearly far from normal for you, '' " This is clearly not your signature, '' " You can see the rest of the stamp lettering on this one. '' Given all of these events we do not feel like our money is safe with PNC Bank and are in the process of moving all our money to another bank.

Product : Credit card Issue : Billing dispute / Chargeback improperly denied Company : Capital One, N.A.

Account : VentureOne Credit Card Case Number : XXXX Amount : {$500.00} Complaint Summary Capital One closed my dispute in favor of the merchant without conducting a reasonable investigation, despite extensive documentation showing non-delivery of services, an unsigned agreement, a fabricated invoice, and an unreachable merchant with no verifiable business address. Capital Ones instruction to work directly with the merchant is unreasonable and impossible, and their decision appears procedurally defective under consumer protection standards. 

Detailed Complaint I am filing this complaint against Capital One, N.A. for failure to conduct a reasonable and fair investigation of my credit card dispute, resulting in an improper denial and rebilling of a fraudulent charge. 

Background On XX/XX/year>, a charge of {$500.00} was billed by XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX for publishing services that were never delivered. I disputed the charge and submitted extensive documentation, including email correspondence, timelines, agreement drafts, and evidence of non-performance. 
Despite this, Capital One closed the case in favor of the merchant on XX/XX/year>, stating that my submission lacked all of the previously requested information. This conclusion is incorrect and unsupported by the record. 

Key Failures by Capital One XXXX. No Signed Agreement The merchant relied on an unsigned agreement to justify performance. The agreement explicitly states it becomes effective only upon execution. I never signed it. Capital One ignored this fact and treated the agreement as binding. 
XXXX. Conditional Emails Mischaracterized as Acceptance Capital One accepted the merchants submission of email screenshots as proof of delivery, despite the emails being explicitly conditional and contingent upon unmet prerequisites. Conditional communications do not constitute acceptance of completed services. 
XXXX. Deliverables Were Not Met The merchant failed to deliver nearly all promised services, including : Website development ISBN registration Publishing platform setup Marketing services Audiobook production Ongoing project management At most, XXXX partial aspect was minimally addressed, which does not justify the charge. 
XXXX. Alleged Deliveries Occurred After Refund Request The merchants claimed deliverables were sent only after I formally requested cancellation and a refund. Capital One did not assess email timestamps showing this sequence. 
XXXX. Spurious Invoice The invoice included in the merchants defense was never issued to me at the time of payment. I repeatedly requested an invoice or receipt and received no response. The invoice appears to have been created solely for the chargeback defense and lacks credibility. 
XXXX. Merchant Is Unreachable The merchant has no verifiable physical address, no functioning phone number, and is unresponsive to email. Capital One nevertheless instructed me to work directly with the merchant, an impossible and unreasonable requirement that effectively denies me recourse. 

Why Capital Ones Decision Is Unreasonable Capital One closed the dispute on procedural grounds without : Addressing merchant non-delivery Accounting for an unsigned agreement Evaluating the validity of the invoice Considering merchant unreachability Weighing post-termination deliveries. 
This constitutes a failure to conduct a reasonable investigation and shifts the burden unfairly onto the consumer.

Sub-issue: Didn't receive terms that were advertised
Consumer complaint narrative:
I am filing this complaint regarding Axos Banks refusal to honor a {$200.00} promotional bonus associated with promo code XXXX, despite my compliance with all disclosed terms and conditions. I opened my business checking account on XX/XX/year> and met the average daily balance requirments for XXXX statement cycle with the first increment of the bonus to be deposited XXXX business days from XXXX cycle closing, which would be around XX/XX/XXXX. 
I relied on Axos Banks promotional representations when opening this business checking account. The promo code was entered during the application process and was a material inducement for opening the account. Axos Bank subsequently approved the account instantly and permitted account activity without requesting any additional documentation. 
After all promotional requirements were satisfied, Axos Bank denied the bonus, asserting ( XXXX ) that the promo code was not used and ( XXXX ) that Articles of Incorporation were not provideddespite the fact that such documentation was never requested during onboarding or at any time prior to denial. 
Promo code XXXX was entered at the time of application. 
Account approval was immediate, with no conditional or provisional status disclosed. 
Axos Bank did not request Articles of Incorporation or notify me that bonus eligibility was contingent upon such documentation. 
Axos Banks denial occurred after the qualifying activity was completed. 
Axos Banks actions raise concerns under unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices ( UDAP ) standards, including but not limited to : Axos Bank failed to clearly disclose any requirement that bonus eligibility depended on additional documentation beyond account approval. Withholding or retroactively asserting material conditions constitutes a deceptive omission. 
Advertising a promotional bonus to induce account opening, then denying payment based on unsupported or undisclosed conditions, is consistent with prohibited bait-and-switch behavior. I reasonably relied on Axos Banks promotional offer and approval process. A banks internal failure to track promo code entry or onboarding documentation can not be shifted to the consumer after reliance has occurred. 
If Axos Bank can not verify promo code usage, this reflects an internal control or system deficiency. Such deficiencies do not excuse non-performance of advertised promotional obligations. Denying a bonus based on documentation never requested prior to or during qualification violates principles of fair dealing and transparent disclosures. 
To ensure accuracy, I restarted the application process prior to submission to confirm that the promo code appeared in the appropriate section of the application, and it did. Only after confirming that the promo code field was present and correctly completed did I proceed with the account opening. 
Based on this diligence, I affirm that the promo code was entered correctly and intentionally. Axos Banks claim that the code was not used is inconsistent with my actions and understanding at the time of application and suggests a system tracking error or internal processing failure rather than consumer error.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am filing this complaint regarding wrongful account closure, inaccurate and inconsistent credit reporting, lack of substantiating evidence, and resulting consumer harm by First Progress Card ( Lead Bank ).

I am currently in the process of purchasing a home, and First Progresss actions have made this process significantly more difficult due to credit score damage and unreliable credit reporting.

First Progress closed my credit card account and reported the account as closed at consumer request. This statement is false. I did not request that my account be closed. To date, First Progress has failed to provide any evidencesuch as a recorded phone call, written request, or signed authorizationshowing that I requested or approved the account closure. 

This wrongful closure caused a significant and immediate drop in my credit score, directly impacting my ability to qualify for mortgage lending. This closure is the originating event that led to all subsequent issues.

A few days later, First Progress reopened the account, yet I received no notice of this action by mail, email, or any other method. I have not been provided proof that any notice was sent. Because I reasonably believed the account was closed due to First Progresss initial error, this lack of notice allowed charges to continue on an account I believed was closed. 

I also did not receive billing statements, payment notices, or requests for payment prior to filing my XXXX  complaint. I further note that I never called to make a payment or acknowledge the debt. I called solely to request a debt validation letter, and I have never agreed that the alleged debt was mine. My call was mischaracterized and improperly relied upon in connection with adverse account actions. 

After disputes were filed, First Progress began quietly changing inaccurate reporting data, which confirms that the information they initially furnished was not accurate. However, correcting data after disputes does not undo the credit damage already caused by their wrongful closure, lack of notice, continued charging, and failure to provide statements. 

Additionally, First Progresss reporting is not consistent across all credit bureaus. Certain bureaus do not reflect the same negative status or delinquency information. This inconsistency further demonstrates inaccurate and unfair credit reporting, not reliable furnishing.

If First Progress can not provide documented proof that I requested the account closure, then the closure itselfand all subsequent adverse reporting and account actions that flowed from itare void and the result of First Progresss negligence. This situation would not exist but for their wrongful initial action. 

Why this is a problem Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), furnishers are required to ensure that information furnished is accurate, verifiable, timely communicated, and consistently reported. 

Closing an account without consumer authorization, reopening it without notice, failing to send billing statements, mischaracterizing consumer communications, and furnishing inconsistent data across credit bureaus constitutes non-compliant and unfair credit reporting practices. 

Quietly correcting inaccuracies after disputes does not satisfy the obligation to explain or substantiate the actions that caused consumer harm, particularly when that harm interferes with a major financial transaction such as a home purchase. 

What I am requesting I am requesting that First Progress be required to : XXXX. Provide documented evidence that I requested the account closure, including call recordings, written requests, or signed authorization. 
XXXX. If no such evidence exists, void the account closure and remove any negative reporting that resulted from it. 
XXXX. Provide documented proof that I was notified of the account reopening, or confirm that no such notice was provided. 
XXXX. Provide a written explanation for : why the account was initially closed, why it was reported as closed at consumer request, why it was reopened without notice, and why reporting differs across credit bureaus. 
XXXX. Correct or remove all inaccurate, inconsistent, or unsubstantiated credit reporting across all credit reporting agencies. 
XXXX. Confirm full compliance with FCRA accuracy, verification, and consumer notice requirements. 


The documents I have provided demonstrate that First Progress has reported inconsistent and inaccurate information across multiple credit reporting agencies. The same account is not reported uniformly, and certain credit bureaus do not reflect the same account status, delinquency information, or historical data. 

Credit reporting agencies are required to receive information that is accurate, complete, and consistent. The discrepancies shown in my supporting documentation confirm that First Progresss reporting does not meet these standards.

This inconsistent reporting further supports that the adverse information furnished by First Progress is unreliable and improperly maintained. If the information were accurate and verifiable, it would be reported consistently across all credit bureaus.

I am requesting that First Progress be required to explain these discrepancies and correct all inaccurate reporting. Any information that can not be fully substantiated must be removed.

This is a follow up to my previous complaint, number XXXX, since your online system did not allow me to leave feedback as requested. The pacifier keeps going round and around until a timeout message appears. I have tried at least a couple times, with no luck. Below is my feedback/reply to Citi 's response : Subject Hello, I am responding to Citis letter in connection with CFPB Case # XXXX. 

Citis response fails to address the core issue raised in my complaint : the misleading way Citis payment system is designed and presented to customers, which reasonably causes consumers to believe they have made an additional or separate payment when, in fact, Citi silently reclassifies that payment as satisfying the Minimum Payment Due.

In Citis online system, when a customer selects Make a Payment, there is no clear, prominent, or meaningful disclosure that the payment will automatically be applied to and subtracted from the Minimum Payment Due, rather than being treated as a standalone payment toward specific balances. This design creates the false impression that the customer has paid amounts over and above the minimum, when in reality Citi later claims the customer has only made the minimum payment. 

This structure is inherently misleading. A reasonable consumer would conclude that making a payment particularly after being instructed by a Citi representative to do so to avoid interest constitutes compliance. Instead, Citis system conceals the remaining obligation, unless the customer logs in frequently, understands Citis internal payment hierarchy, and manually recalculates what Citi will later determine was still owed. This is not transparency ; it is a trap. 

Interest charges do not appear immediately. By the time a consumer discovers the issue when the statement finally generates the damage has already been done. This design effectively guarantees interest accrual while shifting blame to the customer, despite the customer following Citis explicit instructions and acting in good faith.

Citis reliance on generalized Card Agreement language does not cure this problem. Disclosures buried in agreements do not excuse misleading user-interface design, ambiguous payment labeling, or instructions that contradict how payments are actually applied in practice. Consumer protection standards require clarity, not technical compliance that obscures material consequences.

I relied on Citis guidance and on the reasonable interpretation of its payment interface. The interest charged was the direct result of Citis misleading system design and instructions not customer error.

I maintain my request that Citi : Reverse all improperly charged interest, Correct any resulting account impact, and Cease using payment mechanics that mislead consumers into believing they have satisfied their obligations when they have not. 

Payment systems that obscure material information and predictably lead to consumer harm should not be tolerated. Such practices undermine trust, violate the spirit of consumer protection laws, and warrant corrective action.

This is for the same issue that I asked to be investigated before. I have received no response and no acknowledgment from when I asked them to read why they are required by law to treat milestone claims as one continuous transaction. They simply approved two and denied six CONNECTED charges, then closed it due to timeframes, which is not allowed according to their own rules that I will re-list below. 

This is a project that the merchant never delivered on after two years of milestone payments and nine missed deadlines. They have taken over {$38000.00} from me and delivered nothing. 


This is for claims : XXXX, XXXX, XXXX, XXXX, XXXX, and XXXX. 

( Transactions XXXX and XXXX were already refunded. The connected charges were not even looked into because bank employees were unfamiliar with the bank 's timeline procedure for milestone payments ). 


I would also like to note that on at least one of the complaints, a bank employee incorrectly spelled XXXX XXXX as XXXX XXXX XXXX. I had asked it to be fixed, but I don't believe anyone did anything. 


I am disputing the procedural closure of my claims and requesting immediate reopening. The bank improperly applied standard transaction timeframes without addressing delayed discovery, continuous merchant representations, and the fact that all disputed charges arise from one ongoing service contract that resulted in complete non-delivery. 

Banks often deny older disputes by citing standard chargeback windows, but those windows DO NOT apply when : 1. The merchants non-performance was not reasonably discoverable until later 2. Multiple charges are part of a single, continuous contract 3. The merchant retained funds while representing that work was ongoing 4. The consumer made good-faith efforts to resolve directly 5. The product was never delivered All of these apply to my case. They are explicit exceptions in card-network and regulatory guidance.

CFPBs Fair Credit Billing Act, which is federal law, supports this. The key principle is that billing errors include charges for goods or services not delivered as agreed. Most critically, the 60-day notice applies to the initial notice and should not bar investigation when the error was not reasonably discoverable. 

CFPB also repeatedly states that banks must consider ongoing merchant misrepresentation, which is what has been denied to me. In the investigation, all charges were treated as separate but they were all for the same, ongoing project. Since two have been investigated and granted on the grounds of non-delivery, legally, it means the other six related/connected charges should have also been approved.

According to the CFPB supervision manual, the bank must not rely on procedur
al shortcuts such as timeframe does not apply when the facts support ongoing merchant misconduct where one or more of those related purchases is within the timeframe. If one of the charges is in, then ALL connected charges are legally considered within the timeframe.

Denying six connected charges without addressing the relationship between them was a mistake on the Banks part, but a common one that I will ask them to rectify. 

XXXX XXXX XXXX state that that no-delivery equals an ongoing service. It also states that multiple transactions can form one service agreement. This means that the dispute timeframe may be calculated from the date the consumer became aware of non-delivery, not the transaction date. 

According to the Connected Transaction Doctrine, if the payments are milestone-based, all tied to one contract, to the same merchant, and paid with the same promised end product, these charges are REQUIRED to be evaluated together as one purchase, not chopped up to approve some and deny others. Since two of the charges were approved and refunded ( thank you for that ), the other six are also LEGALLY REQUIRED to be refunded due to their milestone connection. 

Due to this, I will formally assert procedural failure on the grounds that the bank improperly closed these disputes. They did so without addressing delayed discovery, continuous merchant representations, and the fact that all disputed charges were part of a single, ongoing service contract that resulted in complete non-delivery.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am submitting this complaint regarding Goldman Sachs Bank USAs handling of my Apple Card billing dispute. 

On XX/XX/year>, I received an email from a third-party auction website ( XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ) stating that I was the winning bidder for a parcel of land ( XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX ) for {$7700.00} . The email stated that if payment was not completed by a deadline, YOUR SALE WILL BE CANCELLED. No penalties, fees, or forfeitures were disclosed in that communication. 

On XX/XX/year>, before making any payment or completing checkout, I contacted the merchant by email and phone to cancel the transaction. I explicitly stated that I could not proceed and that I did not agree to any fee. No goods, services, deed, title, or transfer of property were ever provided to me. 

Despite this cancellation, on XX/XX/year>, the merchant charged my Apple Card {$1000.00}. To justify this charge, the merchant generated a new winning bid entry for a different lot number ( {$1000.00} ) that I never bid on and that does not correspond to any actual property purchase. This charge was not disclosed at checkout, not authorized by me, and not tied to any delivered good or service. 

I disputed the {$1000.00} charge with Goldman Sachs Bank USA under the Fair Credit Billing Act and Regulation Z. During the dispute process, Goldman Sachs repeatedly stated that I agreed to the merchants terms and conditions at the time of purchase. However, no purchase ever occurred. I did not complete checkout, did not submit payment for the land, and did not receive any goods or services. The merchants own emails state that failure to pay results in cancellation, not a penalty. 

Goldman Sachs ultimately denied my dispute and reaffirmed the denial after a reinvestigation, relying on boilerplate language asserting that services were provided or that a purchase occurred. This finding is factually incorrect. There was no completed transaction, no delivery, and no service rendered. Goldman Sachs did not provide me with the merchants evidence, did not reconcile the inconsistency between cancellation and purchase, and did not address the fabricated lot number used to post the charge. 

I believe Goldman Sachs failed to properly investigate my billing error dispute as required by the Fair Credit Billing Act and Regulation Z by : Treating a cancelled transaction as a completed purchase Accepting merchant assertions without addressing contradictory evidence Failing to explain how a charge can be valid when no goods or services were delivered Issuing a conclusory denial without meaningful analysis of the facts presented I am requesting CFPB review of Goldman Sachs Bank USAs dispute handling, investigation process, and compliance with federal billing error protections.

After finally issuing the card, Barclays immediately froze it. Since issuance, the account has been frozen three separate times, each requiring me to call customer service, re-verify my identity using the exact same information and scanned documents they already possess, and obtain manual unfreezing before I can make even one transaction. The online dashboard explicitly states the account is frozen and directs me to call in. Compounding this already unacceptable situation, Barclays online account portal and mobile app provide zero information about current or pending transactions. I can not see what has been spent on the card, view transaction history, check available credit, monitor for unauthorized activity, or even confirm whether a transaction has posted. The dashboard remains blank or shows only frozen status messages with no transactional data whatsoever. Barclays already holds multiple verifications of my identity, scanned copies of my passport, drivers license, utility bills, and my Social Security card ( front and back, sent repeatedly with delivery confirmations ), plus six-plus years of responsible usage, a credit score well above XXXX, and an annual income of {$600000.00}. This is not a technical glitch ; it is a deliberate and material limitation on access that violates federal disclosure and access requirements. 

After six-plus years as a responsible customer and months of enduring their coercive, incompetent, and now opaque process, Barclays must stop harassing me, comply with federal disclosure and access laws, and allow me to use and monitor the credit they issued without further interference.
